Opel's New Astra Start Base Trim Comes With Hub-Capped Steelies Despite Retailing From €31,890
14 photos
Photo: Opel
Opel just made its cheapest Astra a great deal cheaper, and the new Start grade barely gives anything up to shave €1,500 off its predecessor. €1,900 more affordable than before in full-electric flavor, the Start's only real downgrade is the switch to 16-inch steel wheels and some plasticky covers for good measure.
The internal combustion Astra Start and its electric sibling currently start at €31,890 and €36,490 in Germany, including the value-added tax. Patrick Dinger, the head of the brand in Germany, claims the Start is extensively equipped while playing a superior affordability card than many direct competitors. But looking at the bigger picture, over 30,000 euros for a compact still is a lot of money.
Beyond the footwear giveaway, the Start is very similar to the Edition grade. An illuminated Vizor grille is standard, as are LED taillights, LED front lighting units, Intelli-Seats with six-way adjustments and central cushion recesses, LED interior lighting, automatic climate control, and keyless start. Of course, Opel saved a few euros by offering a four-speaker DAB+ radio instead of a higher-quality setup.
Speaking of quality, there are no conventional gauges to speak of. Customers get a pair of 10-inch displays, one handling the instrumentation and the other all things infotainment. Considering that Opel's lesser Frontera Start comes with a smartphone mount instead of an infotainment screen, the Astra Start is the better pick. Front and rear parking sensors also need mentioning, and Opel further made a case for a new paint color.
Denim Blue is a metallic shade that enters the palette at no additional cost. While it may feature basic ADAS, the rearview camera is nowhere to be seen. Thankfully, the rear-facing sensors will come in handy in tight spaces. Another curiosity of the Astra Start is transmission choices. Instead of an honest manual, all powertrains get two-pedal setups.
Photo: Opel The most affordable of Astra Start models is a mild-hybrid turbo 1.2-liter i3 with 143 horsepower to its name. In optimal conditions, this powertrain generates 230 Newton-meters (170 pound-feet) of twist. A six-speed electrified tranny does the shifting. Buyers who do serious highway miles can pick a turbo diesel with around 130 ponies on tap, which includes a torque converter and eight forward ratios.
Upgrading to the Astra Start electric gets you 154 mechanical horsepower and no more than 270 Newton-meters (almost 200 pound-feet) of near-instant torque. Vehicle-to-load capability is listed, though it needs an official adapter. The Start cannot be had as a plug-in hybrid, and that may be a missed opportunity when you remember how versatile PHEVs are.
Available in hatchback and wagon formats, the German model sips 4.7 to 5.1 liters of gasoline per 100 clicks on the WLTP. That's 46 to 50 miles per gallon US. The full-electric alternative packs a 55.4-kWh battery that offers a WLTP-estimated 454 kilometers (282 miles) of range.
Customers who can't do without alloys have to spend an extra €800 for 16s mounted with all-season rubber. The Comfort Pack is the more interesting option, though, for it bundles heat-shielding windows, a center armrest, an auto-dimming function for the central rearview mirror, and wagon-only roof rails.

Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand munitions manufacturing in Grand Prairie, Texas , part of a larger production push that the company says will create 6,000 jobs nationwide, including 2,000 in Texas.
What’s Related
The expansion will bring the Grand Prairie operation’s manufacturing space to more than 735,000 square feet. It includes 100,000 square feet of new space and converting 85,000 square feet of offices into manufacturing space.
Lockheed Martin also announced that manufacturing company Hadrian will install 24 automated machining machines at the facility. Lockheed Martin production employees will operate the equipment, which is expected to begin running in early 2027.
The site makes components for the company’s missile programs and supplies final-assembly operations in locations including Camden, Arkansas, and Troy, Alabama. The expansion adds room for automation and equipment that makes parts to precise measurements.
RELATED STORIES: Amazon Plans Multibillion-Dollar Robotics Plant in Austin | Nvidia and Corning Open New AI Factories in Texas and North Carolina
Converting offices into manufacturing areas
Some of that work is already underway. Lockheed Martin said it has converted former offices into manufacturing areas and installed more than 30 additional precision machines in recent months, with that equipment now producing thousands of components each week.
By the end of 2026, the company expects to have added nearly 100 advanced machines throughout the facility. Nearly 800 production employees currently work there, and the operation manufactured 250,000 parts in 2025.
“Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both,” said Jim Taiclet, the company’s chairman, president and CEO.
Hadrian joins the party
Hadrian’s separate announcement describes a seven-year agreement that builds on a memorandum of understanding announced in December 2025. It brings the company’s automated manufacturing equipment, Opus software , and workforce training into Lockheed Martin’s Grand Prairie operation.
The companies plan to phase in additional groups of machines over the agreement, with each group serving multiple missile programs. Hadrian said the arrangement also allows production to shift among its other factories as demand changes.
The approach puts more component machining inside Lockheed Martin’s own facility while retaining access to Hadrian’s outside factories. Hadrian operates four facilities in California, Arizona, and Alabama.
“The warfighter can't wait on peacetime timelines,” said Chris Power, Hadrian’s CEO.
Part of a larger factory investment
The Grand Prairie project is part of Lockheed Martin’s planned $8 billion to $9 billion investment through 2030 to increase munitions production. That spending includes modernizing or expanding more than 20 U.S. facilities.
Lockheed Martin said agreements covering several missile programs give it greater predictability when investing in employees, equipment, and suppliers.

Do you know the difference between closed-weight models, open-weight models, open-data, and open-source? More importantly, do you think it matters? In a recent webinar, the CEO of CIQ , Gregory Kurtzer, was joined by Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research, to discuss an emerging issue in the AI market: Unknown risk of model failure due to closed-data training. (e.g., not knowing where the model talking to your customers learned its manners, if at all.) The lack of open-data provenance in popular Foundation models may introduce risk for many organizations that are integrating AI into their business processes.
The OpenWALDO project from CIQ is designed to bring “open-data” to the AI training arena as a way to increase trust and reduce risk in the AI market and community. As the webinar transcript describes the project is designed to bring open-data, open-source software, community, and public governance to the mysterious practice of training AI models. Further background can be found in the HPCwire article entitled What is OpenWALDO and Why Did Greg Kurtzer Need to Create It?
The transcript is based on the full video . The following is a shortened transcript that highlights some of the important insights discussed by both Greg and Addison.
Kevin: Welcome, everybody. And thanks for joining us today. We’re going to be talking about OpenWaldo. And you know what it means to have greater visibility and control over the AI models that your organization uses. And, of course, today joining us is Gregory Kurtzer, founder and CEO of CIQ and founder of OpenWALDO. And we also have Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research. My name is Kevin Jackson, and I am an analyst here at Intersect360. Greg and Addison, it’s great to have you here.
Kevin Jackson is an analyst with Intersect360 Research and formerly the editor of AIwire
Greg: It’s good to be here. Thank you, Kevin.
Addison: I always have great conversations with Greg, so this is fun for me. Let’s see how it goes today.
Greg: Absolutely. Great meeting. Interesting or weird.
Addison: You know, we’ll see where we go.
Kevin: Exactly. Well, you know, we’re going to explore what OpenWaldo does. You know why it matters for enterprises and what it could mean for how organizations evaluate and adopt AI going forward. So, you know, just to get us started, I’m going to put this question to both of you. But Greg, I’d like to hear your response first. If I’m running a model on my own infrastructure, I’m keeping my data private. Yeah, I might feel that I’ve handled it or I’ve checked the sovereignty box, but actually what am I still not controlling? And why does that matter?
Greg Kurtzer is the creator of OpenWALD O
Greg: There are a lot of aspects about running your own model, trusting your own model, trusting the infrastructure that that model is running on. And how do you check that box on sovereignty? And it’s even more than sovereignty. It’s ownership, it’s control, and it’s visibility, knowing what it is doing. So a lot of organizations are pulling open-weight models and then running them locally. We don’t know what a lot of these open-weight models have been trained on. We don’t know what they’re going to do in a variety of different situations. We don’t know what the code they’re going to be writing is, or what the interfaces and tooling they’re going to be using are. We don’t know what they’re going to, what it’s going to be doing with it. I mean, that’s kind of, it’s kind of one of the, I’ll say, benefits of a non-deterministic system such as an LLM. But at the same time, even though it’s non-deterministic, they definitely have kind of directions that they will pull toward based on the statistics of what they were trained on. So you need to know kind of what’s inside your model. You need to have proper boundaries, guardrails, and sandboxing of your tooling, your agents, etc., and you need to know what everything is doing. So you need to have proper infrastructure visibility and monitoring.
Addison Snell, CEO of Intersect360 Research
Addison: Yes. I mean, that’s the way we’ve seen it in our research: of course, people are organizations. Enterprises are already moving to adopt AI, as, you know, they want to adopt it. They want the productivity gains. They want the efficiencies. But what I like about what you said, Greg, about control, a lot of that really comes down to risk. And we’ve seen this with any new technology that gets adopted, whether it’s, you know, high-performance computing, modeling and simulation, or whether it’s cloud computing or whether it’s the Internet, right? What are the risks that are involved? And it’s not that I have to have no risk. I just want to know what the boundaries are on the risks. Am I protected on the downside, on cost? Am I protected on the downside on what catastrophe might happen, right? It’s basically the way you put it. And the topic that’s in the popular press right now is all around regulation, the regulatory environment. What we find in our surveys is that people feel like they’re kind of okay with understanding what the different regulatory environments are, but they need to know that they’re stable, right? And, you know, how do I control my intellectual property? How do I control any of my downsides? And that’s what having my own model kind of feels like. It gives me more of a sense of control. I think, you know, regardless of where you stand on the regulatory debate right now, we need more regulation. We need less regulation. I think what a lot of organizations want is predictability. And I think what a lot of organizations want right now is, you know, well, I think the result is: can regulation even stay ahead of AI right now? If I’m going to sit back and wait for regulation to explain everything to me, I’m going to get too far behind. That’s just part of the risk environment right now. So how do I go forward with a model, feel like I have some kind of semblance of control, and manage my risk while I chase the productivity gains?
Greg: You bring up such a good point. A few of them, but one of them that I want to touch on is the data. So for an AI model, whether you’re running it on-prem or you’re running a frontier model, you need to give it data in order to get a good response, right? So inside of your prompt or inside of your tooling, it has to have information about what you want to be asking it. And if you’re asking it things about your core business, core products, trade secrets, things under NDA, like you have to include bits and pieces of that- if not the entire IT in its entirety in your prompt in the context, which means you very well might be leaking data. And this gets really bad when we start talking about agents and, even more than agents, all of the tools that the agents write that are scattered all over the infrastructure or even on the Internet that have access to your data. And then what’s securing those tools, what’s securing those applications, and then what’s securing the agents to make sure that they are being maintained within their guardrails and that we’re not doing something, you know, like hacking another site or hacking a foreign government.
Addison: Well, right. I mean, there are so many analogies with that, that I expect my AI to act within certain boundaries, just like anything else that I hire or employ. If I tell my personal assistant to go pick up my dry cleaning and my personal assistant gets there and finds the dry cleaner to be unexpectedly closed, I don’t expect my personal assistant to smash the windows and break in order to follow the directive to go pick up my dry cleaning, right? Without at least checking with me first. “Hey! It’s closed. Dude, how bad do you need it? Do you want me to write?” That would be outside the normal realm of what I expect. Now, that’s where we talk about guardrails and how the models behave. And I guess you can train a model to do whatever you want. Maybe you’re someone who wants it to go break in, but that should be auditable in some way. Right? Did you give it that directive or not? And you know, when we design a car, we expect it to behave in certain ways. Which doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally cause damage with a car, but you want it to be built so that you don’t accidentally cause damage with a car. I think that’s the point.
Greg: That brings up a whole other can of worms, by the way, which is accountability and liability. And where does that exist? Kevin, I’m going to defer to you on that particular can of worms to keep us on track.
Kevin: I t’s a conversation we’re all having right now. I think something that Addison says all the time, and I’ll fill in here, is that if you use a new technology to commit fraud, it’s not that we need to write a new law. Fraud is already illegal, right? It’s something that Addison brings up quite often — we already have laws in place that perhaps we could be using and strengthening, but it’s a whole debate that could suck up this whole hour if we wanted to.
Addison: Well, I think that’s not the point. Right. But when it comes to control and auditability, there’s been a lot of discussion of things like open weights. But then what’s the difference between open weight and open-source, and what do you get out of it?
Kevin: That’s where I was driving toward. I’m seeing a lot of people use open weight and open-source interchangeably, and they shouldn’t. Greg, can you tell me what the difference is? And why does that difference matter to a company, or a business?
Greg: Well, the first thing that I want to mention is it’s actually really confusing. And it’s confusing because, if you think, I mean, several different aspects, if you think of open-source software, the open-source premise was kind of written around the notion of open-source software. So we kind of have a really good, firm understanding of what that means when we’re applying it to software. You basically think about it as you have the source of something, whether that’s source code or, you know, it’s been debated if data is considered the source in programs, but you have your source, and then you have your output. And if your source is open-source, the output is open-source. Kind of, that’s the definition of open-source, right? With weights, AI weights, it’s different, and it’s different because we have a bunch of open-source tooling that we’re using to build kind of the foundation and architecture of our models. And then we take the input data, the source, which is not open, and use the open-source tools to create binary weights. And these binary weights then are distributed in some cases under an open-source license. So that means you can do whatever you want with the binary weights, but you don’t know what went into those binary weights. The source for it is not available. So I’m a purist when it comes to open-source, in the most fundamental way.
Greg: And as a result of it, I think of it as any source that you’re using to create an artifact needs to be open for that artifact to be called open-source. And so for an AI, that means that your training data- that’s the corpus of data you’re using. It is the composing and the build tools that you’re using to create your model. And if you just have the open weights, well, open weights are great. Please don’t get me wrong on this. I love the fact that we have open weights. A lot of the complaints that we have around open weights, a lot of the concerns, the transparency, Addison, that you were mentioning. Well, the binary weights are kind of like a black box. You can’t ever go from those binary weights. And then understand how they are produced. And so, as a result, we need to kind of be thinking about this from the perspective of what’s inside those, and if we want to mitigate the concerns of what it means to be an open model. Well, we’ve got to go back to the source, and we’ve got to have trust in everything that was used to create this model. And if we have that, then we can fundamentally call ourselves an open-source model, but without that, open-weight models are not bad, but they’re definitely not open-source.
Addison: Yeah. I think what you’re getting at, Greg, is it hits right at that question that we had about mitigating risk because the large organizations or even small organizations we talk to generally have processes in place for when something goes wrong. They want to trace back to how it happened, whether it’s a product defect or a failure in policy somehow. And, you know, there was some customer harm. You want to know not just how to close this gap, but what caused that to happen. What allowed that to happen? And with AI and some of these open-weight models, you don’t know how they were trained. There’s that worry that I’m going to trace it back and I’m going to get back 1 or 2 steps, and the answer is going to be, well, the AI did it, and it stops there. Well, why did the AI do that? And I’d kind of like to know why the AI did what it did, so that I know that I’m not going to repeat the same mistake, which isn’t necessarily really fear-driven. It’s just kind of best practice in any organization to be able to audit why we’re doing the things that we’re doing, particularly in areas that are considered to be strategically important. When we polled organizations, enterprises, medium and up to large enterprises on where they’ve adopted AI, we found it really prevalent in areas like coding and office productivity and, you know, that kind of thing. But it’s least prevalent in areas having to do with product development and engineering and R&D, which is supposed to be the promise of AI, right? It’s going to help us predict the weather and find new products and cure diseases and all these areas that we’re used to associating with high-performance computing and scientific discovery. That’s where AI is least deployed right now. It’s where the biggest gap is. And I think this notion of control and auditability is one of those pieces that’s been missing.
Addison: I mean, look, I’m not a doomer about this. I think there will be things that happen that are bad. Just like with any new technology, if you invent a car, you’re going to have car crashes. Overall, the car accelerates a lot of things and does a lot of good for humanity. Right? And you could say that about any new technology. Overall, I think organizations do want to chase the productivity gains here. People are adopting it. The question I keep coming back to is then: how do I mitigate the risk? How do I control or understand the downside? And in order to activate the upside, because AI should be accelerating discovery in all of these ways, it just feels like there’s been a piece missing to help get to that level of control. That gives me confidence to move it into those areas of forward-leaning R&D and scientific discovery.
Kevin: Absolutely. And, let’s talk about that missing piece. Let’s make it a little bit more concrete with this discussion about OpenWALDO. What can an organization do with OpenWaldo today? And what decision would it help that organization make? How is this going to further that organization’s mission?
Addison: So start by saying what OpenWaldo is. We just dropped this term in here.
Kevin: Please, Greg, why don’t you give us a good, deep discussion of the entirety of this?
Greg: Yeah, absolutely. So kind of going back to the open-source versus the open weights discussion, there isn’t really a way for community members to kind of join together and band together to start creating an AI from scratch. This would involve, as I mentioned before, the AI corpus or training material. This involves data that you’re going to be potentially post-training on and teaching it, for example, how to interact with an API, how to interact with a data structure, how to actually respond properly. So all of these things have to go into the training data, into the corpus. And then you have your tooling, and then all the tooling kind of brings this whole thing together. And then you, of course, need a community around this to be able to say, well, you know, I’m going to bring in this piece of data, or I’m going to work on this tooling, or I’m going to be reviewing this corpus, or I’m going to be looking at the different types of compose files that we have for creating different types of AI models. And I want to ensure, and again, I use this metaphor, tongue-in-cheek humorously, but just to make sure there are no Terminator movie scripts in it or books and whatnot on the AI being not aligned with human humanity and laws, right? So let’s make sure that we are putting laws into this. Let’s make sure that we are putting appropriate ethics into this and having that transparency and visibility. Addison, what you’re mentioning is super important because if I have the ability to choose between two types of models, and I know what went into both of them, I can make an educated decision on which model I want to run, and I can make that decision as a company now, managing some of my risks and compliance.
Addison: I think that’s exactly the point that we were building up to. You’ve created an AI bill of materials that I can investigate, and that the community, as it will, if you think about the open-source community and this becomes an AI community that’s contributing to this corpus, if you’ve got a question about it, take a look. Here it is under the covers. And boy, when I think back to how open-source software really took off, you know, going back to the advent of Linux in the mid to late 1990s, what happened was you had this terrific open-source community of programmers that were then all working on something together. And it didn’t take very long before that raced to the forefront; this is what we’re going to build our organization on.
Greg: The entire free software and open-source movement is that we all have the ability to look at the source for whatever artifacts we’re talking about, right? Whether that source is software. And again, I’m a purist. So whether that source is software and code or whether that’s whatever went into the artifact itself, if you have that ability to see into it, you now have a level of trust that doesn’t require faith. It requires it because you could see it.
Kevin: Absolutely. And this kind of brings me to something I wanted to discuss here. Most companies, most enterprises, most businesses, they’re not training foundation models themselves, right? And if I’m using or maybe fine-tuning someone else’s model, how can OpenWaldo help me? And what would it take to use it in order to benefit my organization?
Greg: T raining a model, I want to say, is a very difficult thing to do. There are a lot of things that can go wrong, and it is exceedingly expensive to have the appropriate hardware to train a model. And an interesting aspect about it is, and I’m just going to kind of talk about this very superficially, but training a model and running your model are two different things, right? So you have your training side, which is where you’re taking all that input data, and you’re kind of managing the orchestration of how you’re building that model, and you’re running it on a very large, very expensive resource, usually with many, many GPUs. On the light side, this is probably tens of millions of dollars to build one of these systems. The large frontier AI labs have ridiculously large investments in their training infrastructure. And I want to be very clear: you could be using that training, that infrastructure, and after months of training, you realize that the model went askew, or your training plan went askew, and you’re either starting over or starting over from the last known good checkpoint. And it’s an expensive, very frustrating, very high-risk kind of process to train a model. And a lot of times you end up with a model that comes out the other side.
Addison: Yes, and the question was around how does OpenWaldo help? And I think you laid the groundwork for that, Greg, because, you know, I don’t really want to train a whole foundation model myself. Let’s take something simple, like a chatbot. I want to use that for my business, whether it’s internal or for my customers. I don’t need to retrain basic human vocabulary from scratch. I do have to give it some knowledge about my products and my business, including my own internal jargon that’s important to me, that might not be in the general corpus, right? So there is some training, but I’d like to start from an auditable, understood foundation because I don’t want to find, you know, later that my chatbot has been, you know, picking up a habit of sexually harassing the people who interact with the chatbot because it learned from the Internet. Right. That would be bad. I don’t want that to happen. I don’t want to train that part. I’d like to have something that comes in starting out good, and then I’m going to specialize it.
Kevin: It’s a great discussion. It’s something that I’m sure we’ll touch back on. But, you know, just to keep this rolling, we’ve kind of been circling around this, but I’d like to dive into it specifically. Say I’m a decision-maker at my company, and I’m deciding on how I want to move forward with the project. How should I decide whether to buy a supported AI product or build on open-source? What should drive that choice?
Greg: So, I’ll jump in on that one. I would make the relation back to what we’ve been doing in open-source for decades now. There are companies that stand behind products that will give you guarantees, assurances, and take the liability on, in many cases, for those products to at least do what those products say that they’re going to do to a reasonable extent. And, when organizations are buying part of their software infrastructure, that’s part of what they’re buying; even if it is 100% based on open-source software, you’re buying that, that commercial relationship; in a more direct sense, you’re buying the throat to choke, and you are mitigating your risks and compliance needs by doing so. Now, if a company wishes to go direct to open-source and download an open-source operating system or build their own kernel or, you know, run without a support contract, without a commercial agreement. I think we found over time that a lot of people did, or what I want is something that’s open-source, but I want a supported version of the open-source, right? But either way, taking the boom in AI now and all of the dialogue we’re already having around open weights and saying, what about something more like open-source with an open corpus and a community-driven effort? I mean, I think this is something that really is going to take off. OpenWaldo is kind of an early mover here; first to market has the opportunity. Is it going to be OpenWALDO in the future? I guess that’s for CIQ and to try to drive their product. But we haven’t seen this before. And I think for those who are worried about, you know, us or Western technology and what’s going on with the Chinese, I mean, you know, imagine if this were a Chinese product right now, would there be concern about what the control around it is and who’s auditing it? I think the idea that you have an open community, open corpus, open weight, open-source, like, here’s something I can understand and build AI on it. Companies will evaluate how much control, how much support they want over time. But an open community effort around AI, I think we’ve seen enough in the past to know that this is an idea that ought to take off.

It’s because, well, maybe, but it’s because WALDO stands for open weights, open artifacts, open licenses, open data, and open origins. How do we build the confidence that the simulation is good? It rhymes with the idea that how do I build confidence that the AI is good means evolving my process. You know, if I have a customer service rep, I train them, and I monitor them to make sure that they’re interacting with the customer the right way. Chatbot, same thing, right? I want to train them. Inconsistent reporting at a Pennsylvania site affected microbiological analyses of components and drug products that analytical testing service provider Eurofins ran for customers.
The FDA has hit Eurofins with a warning letter after the contract testing laboratory admitted “selectively recording test results.”
Eurofins performs microbiological analyses of components and drug products for customers. Across a business that serves multiple industries, Eurofins employs more than 65,000 people across more than 950 laboratories in 57 countries. The FDA observed compliance failings when it visited the company’s laboratory in Horsham, Pennsylvania, in June.
Inspectors found Eurofins failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data from tests needed to ensure regulatory compliance. The concerns centered on pour plates for counting microorganisms.
Responding to the FDA, Eurofins said that analyst interviews and a retrospective review of laboratory data showed inconsistent reporting practices dating back to February 2025. The company acknowledged that some analysts were selectively recording test results, only documenting pour plate results in certain circumstances.
The FDA deemed Eurofins’ response inadequate for addressing the issues identified by agency inspectors. One inspector saw a Eurofins microbiologist fail to record results, according to the warning letter. The inspector also noted cracked and desiccated pour plate samples, which could no longer reliably support uniform microbial growth.
“A result recorded from a compromised plate, even one that falls within specification, cannot be considered valid, as the physical condition of the media may have suppressed or obscured actual microbial recovery,” the agency said.
The FDA also found fault with Eurofins’ data review procedure. One failing illustrated “the unreliability of your data, and further demonstrates that lack of secondary verification is unacceptable,” the FDA said.
Another section of the warning letter focused on Eurofins’ failure to thoroughly investigate the cracked or desiccated plates used for testing raw material and drug product samples. The company told the FDA that it investigated the scope of affected samples and the adequacy of results. Based on analyst interviews and a limited records review, Eurofins concluded the results were valid, according to the letter.
The FDA again found Eurofins’ response inadequate. Lacking photographic evidence of plate conditions, the agency saw no basis to retroactively confirm any results. Eurofins’ conclusions relied solely on analyst interviews and data records that the company acknowledged are unreliable, the FDA said.
“Data integrity depends on complete and accurate documentation of test results and conditions. Failure to maintain such records undermines the reliability of your data,” the agency wrote to Eurofins. “The use of deficient media similarly compromises the validity of microbiological test results and raises questions about the suitability and robustness of your methods.”
Eurofins was one of several companies to receive a manufacturing-related warning letter in the FDA’s latest batch of compliance notices. The FDA also issued warning letters to Korea’s Hanlim Pharm and the U.S. 503B outsourcing facility SCA Pharmaceuticals. FDA inspectors found poor aseptic practices and inadequate cleaning at Hanlim’s plant. SCA received its warning letter for drug compounding failures.

The open pit at the former Jeffrey asbestos mine in Quebec. Credit: Credit: Chilanga Cement/Wikimedia Commons
Posted By: Blair McBride October 16, 2026
Few chapters in Quebec’s mining history are as dramatic as that of asbestos, first discovered near Thetford in the province’s southeast in 1876. Three years later, another major find about 60 km away produced the Jeffrey mine. The town of Asbestos (now Val-des-Sources) grew around it.
Used as a cheap source of insulation and fireproofing, commercial asbestos mining expanded into the 20th century in clusters around Thetford and Asbestos. More than a dozen operations – mostly open-pit – grew by the 1930s.
World leader
In 1930, The Northern Miner reported that Quebec mines had extracted 5.1 million tons of asbestos-bearing rock in 1929. The previous year, shipments of processed asbestos totalled $11.2 million in value – about $203 million today – several times the amount of any competing country.
“Canada supplies about 70% of the world’s asbestos from a serpentine belt running through the Eastern townships of the province of Quebec to the Vermont border,” The Miner reported in 1943.
But medical knowledge was less advanced in the early 20th century, and asbestos soon faced a reckoning.
Alarming medical report
Most long-term workers at Quebec asbestos mines suffered from lung problems, including cancer, from breathing in asbestos fibres, a 1975 report from Mount Sinai Hospital in New York stated. That sparked a strike in Thetford, where thousands of employees walked off the job demanding better working conditions.
In the following decades, Quebec’s asbestos industry declined as growing evidence of its health risks prompted stricter regulations and curtailed demand.
It all came to an end in 2010 when the Jeffrey mine closed. Almost all of its last 150,000 tonnes of asbestos – worth $90 million – went to developing countries.
The Quebec government made an awkward, last-ditch attempt to reopen Jeffrey in 2012 as an underground operation, even approving a $58-million loan for it. But the newly elected Parti Québécois government withdrew the financing, finally closing Quebec’s asbestos chapter.
This is part of The Northern Miner ‘s From The Archives series, where we link current developments, like rising precious metals prices incenting further exploration and mining, with news items from our 111 years of archives. The Miner is one of Canada’s oldest mining publications.

Europe's Auto Industry Faces New Trade-Off Between Emissions Rules and Local Production
18 photos
Photo: Ineos
Britain could join the Made in Europe club for EU automotive support in the near future, and the kicker is that the United Kingdom could enjoy this membership without rejoining the European Union. There is, however, a catch. London may have to align with Brussels on trade measures targeting Chinese newcomers, and in the process, it may have to surrender certain freedoms to set its own import policy in exchange for access to Europe's industrial support schemes.
Reported by Reuters, the condition is part of a provisional bargain prompted by France and Germany. This deal could give automakers more flexibility over the incoming 2035 auto emissions regulations. Both Paris and Berlin have been trying to settle a dispute that pits Germany's preference for more room to sell internal combustion vehicles against France's push for European-centric manufacturing.
This emerging compromise links the goals of both parties instead of treating them as separate problems. Looking at the bigger picture, Made in Europe is less about European automotive pride than deciding where that extremely sweet public money goes. The proposed rules would affect products brought through subsidy schemes, public procurement, and public auctions.
As far as France is concerned, Paris has pushed for a narrow definition limited to the member states of the union. Germany has argued that countries closely integrated with European supply chains should qualify as well. Under the compromise in question, the proposed rules would cover the European Union's member states and permit other European partners that previously belonged to the single market to opt in, thus opening the door to the UK.
For British automakers like Bentley, MINI, Rolls-Royce, and Jaguar Land Rover, the opportunity is pretty obvious. So is the condition attached to it, though, for the draft calls for complete reciprocity and alignment with EU rules covering investments from third countries and trade defense. Put into practice, Britain would have to follow European restrictions on Chinese-built vehicles and all future measures affecting Chinese imports.
Photo: Renault Brexiters may find this awkward, especially when you remember that the UK's government has successfully resisted the pressure to copy EU tariffs on Chinese vehicles. France dropped its opposition to British inclusion earlier this week, but only with the condition that London aligns with the bloc's trade defense policy.
Advantages within the union are pretty clear, all the while Britain greatly nerfs its freedom to diverge on some trade measures. The emissions side of the deal is the most consequential for automakers, though its precise mechanisms have yet to be detailed. Under the current framework, the fleet-wide target from 2035 represents a 100 percent reduction in CO2 emissions against the EU's 2021 baseline.
Per a December 2025 European Commission automotive package, the 2035 deadline may result in a 90 percent tailpipe emissions reduction. The remaining 10 percent would be compensated through low-carbon steel made in the union or alternative fuels. According to Reuters, the Franco-German plan would keep the 90 percent reduction target while removing the need for those additional compensating measures, making compliance less restrictive.
Furthermore, this proposal would also leave more room for internal combustion and plug-in hybrid vehicles after 2035. While not a rollback of emissions rules or a straightforward protectionist pact, this proposal goes to show that both France and Germany care about their automotive industries a lot more nowadays than they did back when everyone thought that electric vehicles would reign supreme by 2030.

Electric Chevrolet Corvette Coming, GM Doesn't Know When
8 photos
Photo: General Motors
Chevrolet offers the Corvette in all sorts of flavors. Rear-wheel drive with zero electrification, all-wheel drive with electric motors, going from 535 horsepower all the way to a mind-blowing 1,250 horsepower. General Motors has one more variant in the pipeline, and that’s an electric Corvette.
Before you panic, you must know that the arrival of an electric Corvette will by no means affect the lineup with internal combustion engines. V8s are obviously here to stay. So, yes, an all-electric Chevrolet Corvette is officially still in the pipeline, but it is not coming anytime soon. We have been hearing this for at least a decade.
General Motors' Executive Chief Engineer for Corvette and Performance Cars, Tony Roma, clarified that while fully electric vehicles are " the end game ," a zero-tailpipe-emission Corvette is inevitable. However, the auto giant has no immediate timeline for its release.
" Someday, we will fully electrify Corvette. But not today ," Roma concluded. While GM originally teased an electric model back in 2015 , the automaker anticipated the EV meltdown and decided to stick to V8s with or without electric assistance rather than rushing headfirst into an all-electric lineup.
Photo: Chevrolet Now, GM President Mark Reuss confirmed for CNBC the arrival of another electrified Chevrolet Corvette next year, followed by an electric version of the sports car. However, he hasn't disclosed any timeline for its arrival. As for the electrified Corvette, we will live to see if it will be a hybrid or a plug-in hybrid.
For the moment, the only electrified Corvettes are the Grand Sport X, which replaced the outgoing E-Ray, and the ZR1X hypercar, rocking totally distinct setups and totally different amounts of power, but both sporting all-wheel drive.
The Grand Sport X received the new 6.7-liter LS6 naturally aspirated engine and a permanent-magnet electric motor mounted on the front axle. Together they produce 721 horsepower (731 metric horsepower) and 665 pound-feet (902 Newton meters) of torque.
Those are enough to make it rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.4 seconds, run the quarter mile in 10.4 seconds wth a trap speed of 129.2 mph and max out at 190 mph (306 kph). An eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission sends power to the ground through all four corners. Customers can get all those for a starting price of $110,000.
Photo: Chevrolet In the meantime, the other electrified Corvette, the almighty ZR1X, sits at the top of the lineup with a starting price of $227,800. It is the most expensive production Corvette ever built, but also the most powerful of them.
That is because the 5.5-liter twin-turbocharged flat-plane crank LT7 V8 works alongside the front-axle permanent-magnet electric for a combined output of 1,250 horsepower (1,267 metric horsepower) and 973 pound-feet (1,320 Newton meters) of torque.
Those are the figures that make it flash from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in just 1.68 seconds on a fully prepped drag strip surface (1.89 seconds with no preparation), run the quarter mile in 8.67 seconds and top out at 233 mph (375 kph).
To make sense in this lineup, an electric Corvette should be close to that sort of performance. In the meantime, General Motors is well aware that another $200,000 Corvette wouldn’t exactly sell like hotcakes.

Environmental groups warn seabed mining may harm fragile marine habitats and disrupt ecosystems. ( Stock image by magdal3na. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 16, 2026
Metal-rich rocks recovered from the Pacific Ocean began smoking and heating when researchers broke them apart in a laboratory, highlighting a potential fire hazard for mining seafloor sulphide deposits.
Two of 57 hydrothermal rock samples collected during a 2022 expedition to the Escanaba Trough, off the Oregon–California border, spontaneously combusted after freeze-drying. Temperatures exceeded 100 C and the original samples completely oxidized, according to a study led by the U.S. Geological Survey in Scientific Reports .
“The production of heat through exothermic reactions has not been investigated in SMS deposits but has the potential to cause rapid onset fires on ships,” the researchers wrote, referring to seafloor massive sulphide deposits, in research outlined Oct. 7 by the federal agency.
The findings highlight handling considerations specific to deposits formed around hydrothermal vents, where mineral-rich fluids meet cold seawater. These differ in composition and structure from the polymetallic nodules targeted by The Metals Company (Nasdaq: TMC) and Deep Sea Minerals (CSE: SEAS).
Unstable minerals
Researchers collected the rocks using a remotely operated vehicle to investigate four regions of the Escanaba Trough. Forty-one samples contained metal sulphides as a major component.
The two that combusted were dominated by nanocrystalline marcasite, a form of iron sulphide made up of extremely small crystals. It had replaced an earlier mineral, pyrrhotite, while preserving its blade-like shape.
That transformation left small crystals and pore spaces that could increase contact with oxygen and make the material more reactive.
The researchers examined whether petroleum-like material associated with the deposits could explain the combustion. Their analyses instead pointed to reactions involving the sulphide minerals.
The laboratory handling offers an important qualification. The rocks had been freeze-dried, and the two reactive samples began generating noticeable heat and smoke when broken by hand to fit inside a crushing vessel, before the mechanical crusher started.
The laboratory results offer an early indication of how particular seabed minerals may react during processing, with further testing needed to assess their behaviour under commercial operating conditions.
Shipboard risks
Self-heating and combustion of sulphide ores are already documented in terrestrial mining. The question is whether younger seabed deposits, with different mineral textures and environmental conditions, require different precautions.
The authors suggest they may. Modern seafloor sulphides have undergone much less compaction and geological alteration than ancient deposits mined on land, potentially leaving them more reactive.
How operators handle the material could also matter. Breaking rocks underwater could allow heat to dissipate and reduce the risk of self-heating. Further crushing aboard ships or excessive removal of water could increase it.
The authors call for dedicated risk assessments and engineering controls if mining of seafloor massive sulphide deposits proceeds, with the characteristics of individual deposits guiding precautions.
“The new research suggests that some SMS rocks have physical and chemical properties that could make them behave very differently from comparable mineral deposits mined on land,” the agency said.

source_document.body:

Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 16, 2026
The global refined copper surplus is expected to more than triple next year as production growth outpaces consumption, despite demand from electrification, artificial intelligence and data centres, the International Copper Study Group says.
The surplus is forecast to reach 368,000 tonnes in 2027, up from 104,000 tonnes this year, the Lisbon-based intergovernmental group said in its October forecast . Next year’s excess would represent about 1.3% of global consumption, with refined output of 29.7 million tonnes against usage of 29.3 million tonnes.
Refined production growth is expected to accelerate to 3.4% in 2027 from just 0.4% this year, exceeding projected consumption growth of 2.5%. The rebound would be supported by smelter and refinery ramp-ups in Indonesia, India and the European Union, improved operating rates in Chile and increased production from scrap.
The outlook points to a widening surplus of refined metal even as disruptions at major mines restrict supplies of copper concentrate used by smelters. Recovering mine output and growing scrap production are expected to help ease those constraints next year.
The 2026 surplus estimate is slightly higher than the 96,000 tonnes projected in April, while next year’s forecast is broadly in line with the earlier outlook.
Mine supply recovery
World copper mine production is expected to grow by 1.3% this year, down from the 1.6% projected in April following downward revisions to output in Chile, China and Indonesia.
Growth is being supported by ramp-ups at Rio Tinto’s (LSE, NYSE, ASX: RIO) Oyu Tolgoi mine in Mongolia, Amman Mineral Internasional’s (IDX: AMMN) Batu Hijau mine in Indonesia and privately held Russian Copper’s Malmyz mine in Russia.
Expansions at Zijin Mining’s (HKEX: 2899; SSE: 601899) Julong mine in China and Ural Mining and Metallurgical’s Svyatogor operations in Russia are also contributing, alongside higher output at Peru’s Antamina, jointly owned by BHP (LSE, NYSE, ASX: BHP), Glencore (LSE: GLEN), Teck Resources (TSX: TECK.B; NYSE: TECK) and Mitsubishi (TSE: 8058), and processing of stockpiled ore at First Quantum Minerals’ (TSX: FM) Cobre Panama.
Production remains constrained at Freeport-McMoRan’s (NYSE: FCX) Grasberg mine in Indonesia and Kamoa-Kakula in the Democratic Republic of Congo, jointly owned by Ivanhoe Mines (TSX: IVN; US-OTC: IVPAF), Zijin Mining and other partners, following incidents in 2025. Declining Chilean mine output is also limiting global growth.
Refined copper production from scrap is forecast to increase by about 4.7% in 2027, while primary refined output from mined copper is expected to rise by around 3%.
Demand growth lags
Global refined copper usage is projected to increase by 1.5% this year and 2.5% next year, with Asia remaining the main source of growth.
China, which accounts for 59% of global refined copper consumption, is expected to increase apparent usage by 2.5% this year, while usage across the rest of the world remains essentially unchanged.
The Chinese calculation uses reported production, net trade and changes in Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks. It excludes changes in unreported inventories held by state agencies, producers, consumers and traders, which can materially alter the global supply-demand balance, the group cautioned.
The ICSG lowered its 2026 consumption growth outlook slightly from April, citing weaker expectations for the Middle East, North America and the European Union. Demand in Japan is also expected to remain subdued.
Consumption growth next year should benefit from an anticipated improvement in global economic activity, new and expanded plants making semi-finished copper products such as wire, tube and sheet, and stronger operating rates at those plants in the Middle East.
The forecasts remain vulnerable to supply disruptions and geopolitical developments, particularly the conflict in the Middle East, which could affect both production and consumption, the group said.

The Port of Long Beach moved 997,177 twenty-foot-equivalent units in September, its busiest month in 115 years and a 25% increase from September 2025, port officials said Thursday.
The total surpassed the port’s previous monthly record of 987,191 TEUs, set in October 2024.
Port Chief Executive Noel Hacegaba said shippers increasingly relied on Long Beach as they adjusted to high diesel costs, Panama Canal access restrictions and the prospect of a new U.S.-China trade agreement. He said the record came with no congestion .
Loaded imports rose 31.3% year over year to 509,390 TEUs, while exports increased 7.8% to 91,747 TEUs. Empty container moves climbed 22.1% to 396,040 TEUs.
Through the first nine months of 2026, the port handled 7,675,255 TEUs, up 3.9% from the same period in 2025.
Hacegaba highlighted Total Terminals International, which set a Port of Long Beach monthly rail record in September by handling 59,410 moves, nearly half of the terminal’s total container volume.
The port also announced an incentive program ahead of Caltrans’ planned 16-month deck-replacement project on the Vincent Thomas Bridge, which begins Nov. 7. Starting in late October, Long Beach container terminals will offer additional evening and Saturday gates for six weeks, excluding Thanksgiving week, to give truckers more flexibility during the closure.
The port expects to remain fully open while the bridge project proceeds at the neighboring Port of Los Angeles.

A Maersk methanol-fuelled ship
By Alison Koo
16 October 2026
Shipping lines claim they are bearing the cost of investments in alternative fuels and lower-emission vessels, as shippers and their freight forwarders remain reluctant to pay more for greener shipping.
That is according to speakers at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference and Exhibition yesterday.
Pacific International Lines (PIL) head of operations and procurement (China) Chia Yujin said shippers in price-sensitive markets were not yet ready to pay for the industry’s transition to alternative fuels by 2050, leaving carriers to finance much of the investment.
In March 2022, PIL was the first Asian shipping line to commission LNG dual-fuelled ships, ordering four 14,000 teu vessels at Jiangnan Shipyard.
“Our ships trade in Latin America, we trade to Africa, and usually our shippers are from China,” Mr Chia said.
“At this point in time, people are a little bit more price-sensitive. Our shippers and consignees are typically not very ready to pay for the transition, so everything we do has to be voluntary, and come out from our own pocket,” he added.
Despite the lack of immediate financial returns, shipping lines are pressing ahead with alternative-fuel vessels and investing in the operational expertise needed to use them, it was said.
X-Press Feeders’ head of global operations, Vijayachelvan Silva Raju, said the company deployed methanol-powered ships without customers sharing the additional costs, partly to prepare its workforce for a future in which alternative fuels are expected to play a larger role.
And the world’s largest feeder operator is investing in crew training, building a pool of personnel experienced in handling methanol; Mr Raju argued that waiting until demand increased could leave it without sufficiently trained crews.
“We don’t have any shippers we could share the cost with. But why are we still operating these ships? Because we believe that when it comes to 2030, we will need to operate more ships with the same fuel, and I can’t go and find a trained crew at that time. So we are investing now, not just in assets, but also on crew and training,” he explained.
There are now 650 containerships capable of using alternative fuels including methanol and liquefied natural gas (LNG) on order, compared with around 330 in September 2023.
Maersk Line has 56 dual-fuelled ships on order and is already operating 24. Its head of fleet operations (East), Dinesh Kumar Balraj, said alternative fuels must be available at commercially viable prices, while ports need suitable bunkering facilities and ship operators must ensure their crews are trained to handle them.
“It’s not just placing orders for dual-fuelled vessels, but also how we optimise the existing fleet through retrofitting or other methods like digitalisation and network optimisation,” he said. “Now it’s about scaling what we’ve learned – we’ve had a lot of experience operating dual-fuelled vessels, learning about different fuels.
“Scaling doesn’t mean that an engine has to run on a particular fuel. The fuel and the bunkering infrastructure should be available; operationally, we must be ready, and the crew must be ready,” he added.

There are plenty of e-bike conversion kits designed to turn your existing bicycle electric, but most involve at least a bit of wrenching. Spiny 2 takes a different approach, using a removable friction-drive system that can apparently snap onto your bike in just three seconds.
Now let me start by saying that this is a crowdfunding project on Kickstarter, so it’s a “buyer beware” situation. My long-time readers will know I have a rule about crowdfunding campaigns. I don’t cover them unless they either A) come from a company that has a track record of delivering products in the past, or B) I personally test out the product in advance to confirm it’s legitimate and works. In this case, I haven’t personally tested the Spiny 2 e-bike kit, but the brand does appear to have delivered hundreds of their previous version of the kit, so this isn’t a brand new, fly-by-night company.
The newly unveiled second-generation system combines its motor and battery into a compact 2.2 kg (4.9 lb) package. Once the mounting hardware and sensors are initially installed on the bike, the entire drive unit can be clicked into place before a ride and removed afterward.
It’s a friction drive kit, which isn’t the most elegant way to drive an e-bike, but it does get the job done quickly and simply.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That could be particularly useful for riders who want to keep the feel of their favorite pedal bike, but occasionally want a little electric help.
Instead of replacing a wheel or integrating with the drivetrain, Spiny 2 uses a roller that contacts the rear tire. Cadence and speed sensors detect when the rider begins pedaling, at which point the motor moves against the tire and begins providing assistance in around 0.25 seconds. Stop pedaling and the roller lifts away again, allowing the bike to roll without additional motor drag.
Keeping the whole kit street lega, the US version is rated at 250W nominal but can produce up to 750W of peak power and assist riders up to 20 mph (32 km/h). Canadian models peak at 500W, while versions intended for most other markets are limited to 250W and 25 km/h (15.5 mph).
A 266Wh battery is built into the removable unit, with Spiny claiming up to 90 km (56 miles) of range under ideal conditions. As always with e-bike range figures – especially one that ambitious from a relatively small battery – expect real-world range to depend heavily on assist level, terrain, rider weight, and speed. Suffice it to say though that unless you’re doing pro-level pedaling by yourself, the 266Wh battery isn’t going to net normal folks like you and me anywhere close to 56 miles of range on average day.
There are five pedal-assist levels controlled through a smartphone app or optional Bluetooth handlebar remote. Charging is handled via USB-C PD, while the unit carries an IP65 weather-resistance rating. That USB-C charging is perhaps one of the nicest features on the whole kit, allowing convenient recharging from a typical laptop charger or even a powerbank, and helping the kit join a very limited club of USB-C rechargable e-bikes.
Compatibility is fairly broad, including many road, city, hybrid, and touring bikes with either rim or disc brakes. Adapters are also available for some tighter-clearance bikes and Bromptons, though rear-suspension bicycles are excluded.
There are some limitations, with a major one being that you can’t operate a normal rear fender (though the higher floating style rear fenders should likely still work).
Spiny 2 recently launched on Kickstarter , with deliveries currently estimated for April 2027.
As with any crowdfunded hardware product, those delivery dates aren’t guarantees. But if Spiny can deliver on its promises, the ability to electrify your existing bike for Monday’s commute and turn it back into a normal lightweight bicycle three seconds later is certainly an interesting proposition.

The latest edition of the Paris Motor Show gave AITO the chance to put a few models on display in front of potential customers, with the company showing off the 9, 8, 7, and 6 sport utility vehicles. 9 is the largest of the bunch, measuring just over 5.2 meters (206 inches) between the front and rear bumpers and 3.1 meters (122 inches) between the front and rear axles.
Based on these dimensions, the 9 would have to prove itself against the likes of the Mercedes-Benz GLS, BMW X7, and the Audi brand's Q9. The powertrain strategy is to give customers a choice between electric and extended-range electric powertrains, with the latter being a setup in which the combustion engine is there solely to generate electricity rather than driving the wheels.
EREVs were designed specifically for the kind of customer who wants electric driving without any charging-related compromises. On longer journeys where the charging infrastructure may not be good enough for a trouble-free driving experience, the onboard generator saves the day as long as there is dinosaur juice in the fuel tank.
As noted earlier, the European lineup remains a work in progress. Displaying four vehicles in the French capital is not the same as confirming those four models for sale in the union, and AITO has not named the initially targeted markets either. For the time being, the Chinese newcomer is approaching groups willing to represent it.
Photo: AITO The dealership network is especially important for customers in this particular segment, for premium SUV buyers expect somewhere to take their vehicles for servicing, a healthy supply of replacement parts in the event of a fender bender, and technicians capable of repairing all hardware or software issues. If you ask me, aftersales concerns me just as much as quality when it comes to Chinese vehicles. This and other concerns are why the dealership network matters so much.
AITO's pitch for Europe leans heavily on software, which is hardly attractive to anyone who simply wants a dependable vehicle. Gifted with Huawei goodies, including the Harmony operating system and choice advanced driver assistance features, AITO models lean a lot more into all things technology than their supposed German rivals from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi .
Before selling prospective customers the technology promise, AITO has to adapt its driver-assistance system for local roads and Europe's specific driving conditions. At press time, the company is working toward type approval and five-star Euro NCAP safety ratings under the 2026 testing protocols.
AITO claims to have accumulated 40 billion kilometers (24.9 billion miles) to date, of which more than 10.6 billion clicks (6.6 billion miles) were driven with some degree of driver assistance. Manufacturer-reported figures mean little, though, especially when prospective customers from Europe don't know how the automaker's systems behave on their own roads.
Another hurdle AITO has to consider is the import bill. Its Chinese-built vehicles would face an EU tariff of 30 percent under current rules, and that levy alone convinced a bunch of Chinese automakers to invest big money in European production facilities. Given that the brand currently lacks a high-volume model that would justify building one, European production doesn't seem likely by decade's end.

WASHINGTON — The Association of the United States Army showcased its annual conference from Oct. 12-14 in Washington, assembling defense industry officials, lawmakers and military personnel from around the globe to assess the future force and evolving threats.
Dominating displays at this year’s show was an unmistakable surge in automation and unmanned systems, as well as weaponry and vehicle capabilities that continue to adapt to a frenzied pace of innovation at the heart of today’s conflicts.
Army officials attending the conference emphasized the service’s need for rapid transformation as the technologies at the core of these conflicts seemingly evolve by the day.
Defense News and Army Times covered these discussions — and more — from this year’s show.
Catch up on all of our top stories from this year’s AUSA conference and be sure to read our latest coverage at defensenews.com/digital-show-dailies/ausa .

Drone dominance
A drone swarm returns from a mission during the XVIII Airborne Corps’ Scarlet Dragon 26-3 at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on Sept. 15, 2026. (Pfc. Iliana Lopez/U.S. Army)
Pentagon, Army go all in on autonomy
The Pentagon wants to take its stockpile of autonomous weapons from thousands of units into the millions.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed AUSA attendees at the Project Agincourt panel on Wednesday, sharing that the Pentagon is requesting roughly $50 billion in reconciliation funding to support the push to scale autonomous and robotic systems. Read more here .
Autonomous weapons are changing the way brigades fight
At Fort Bragg, soldiers recently tested how unmanned systems could help troops breach obstacles while reducing exposure to battlefield hazards.
During Project Sandhills 2.0 , soldiers planned flight routes and operated Bumblebee V2 small unmanned aircraft systems at Range 63.
The project tested how unmanned systems could support contested obstacle breaching, while soldiers and industry partners collected feedback to inform future Army capabilities. Read more here .
US Army to stand up command for unmanned and autonomous warfare
The U.S. Army ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems a day after Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare.
An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM. It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems. Read more here .
US Army expands drone marketplace to 33 nations
The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally.
Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday.
Since the marketplace was stood up, it has processed $800 million in transactions. Read more here .
Drone carrying M250 machine gun completes firing test
A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday.
Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount. Read more here .
US Army targets 2028 for first high-energy laser counter-drone weapons
The first directed energy weapon selected by the U.S. Army for the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program could be out of testing and ready for counter-drone operations by early 2028, Army officials told Military Times.
In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system. Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment. The first LOCUST X3 is slated for delivery by Q4 of FY 2027 and will be mounted on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Read more here .

A forward-looking philosophy
The Washington, D.C.-based startup Rivet is developing militarized smart glasses for the U.S. Army. (Rivet)
‘Noticeable shift in warfare’: Army under secretary on the lessons of modern combat
The Army’s evolving priorities were reflected all over the AUSA show floor, according to Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal. In a sit-down with Military Times , Obadal highlighted areas that look nothing like the armor-heavy shows of years past.
Obadal also discussed the high-low mix of exquisite and affordable munitions, faster acquisition cycles and why keeping a human in the loop remains the default for AI on the battlefield. Read more here .
‘We’ve drowned ourselves in buzzwords’: Acting secretary gives sermon-like first speech
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle’s AUSA speech differed significantly from his predecessor’s in 2025, but he quickly made it clear that the Army was holding the course set by former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned Aug. 31 over growing disagreements and friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Telle hailed the Army’s work to streamline acquisition and reduce roadblocks to getting soldiers the gear they need, citing the Army’s work to reduce service “fiefdoms” from thousands to a few newly named portfolio acquisition executives. Read more here .
The Army’s new warfare guidance
Disrupt enemy command and control. Hit enemy forces with firepower , then assault with ground troops to finish the job. And be resilient enough to function despite what the enemy dishes out in return.
That’s the essence of “How The Army Fights,” a new 46-page guide on how the U.S. Army can leverage the tactical to improve the operational . Read more here .
9 companies selected to build next-gen command and control software
The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software.
The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software.
The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield. Read more here .
A second expeditionary cyber battalion on the horizon
The Army will soon double the number of battalions it uses to train and deploy expeditionary cyberspace and electromagnetic warfare teams, according to the Army.
At AUSA on Monday, head of Army Cyber Command Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank gave an approximate timeline for when the service would be delivering the new unit devoted to the exact same mission as the 11th Cyber Battalion, dubbed the Leviathans. Read more here .
An Indo-Pacific manufacturing hub in Korea?
As the Eighth Army in Korea builds out its logistics capability, it’s investing in advanced manufacturing with an eye to supplying spares, not only to local Army forces, but also to troops across the Pacific region .
Eighth Army officials spoke earlier this year about how establishing a Korea-based regional sustainment hub, or center for logistics, maintenance and supply, could cut down the burden and cost of long-distance sustainment. At a roundtable event Monday, Eighth Army Commander Lt. Gen. Joseph Hilber indicated the force was moving out to build that sustainment hub. Read more here .

Weapons and equipment
An XM8 at a weapons range at Fort Benning, Georgia. (Pfc. Kiana Tyson/U.S. Army)
M8 rifle to begin fielding in December
Fielding of the M8 carbine, which appears set to replace Sig Sauer’s M7 as the Army’s standard rifle less than three years after the M7’s initial fielding began, will begin in December with some units at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, company executives confirmed to Military Times.
The NGSW new weapons rollout also includes Sig’s M250 machine gun, which will replace the aging M249 Squad Automatic Weapon and is expected to reach troops in the first half of next year, said Dave Buehler, the company’s vice president of manufacturing. Read more here .
A 25-round mag for Army’s next-gen rifle
Soldier feedback, from the constructive to the blistering, has been instrumental in guiding weapons manufacturer Sig Sauer in its development of the M8 carbine.
Among those changes is a 25-round magazine to replace the 20-round mag that shipped with the M7, said Josh Shoemaker, Sig’s product manager for defense. Read more here .
US Army gets first mobile cannon to replace M777 howitzer
The U.S. Army has taken delivery of its first Korean-made mobile tactical cannon less than a year after first issuing a solicitation, service officials said.
Speaking to reporters, the Army’s leader for offensive fires said that the mobile tactical cannon, made by Hanwha Defense USA , was on display at a first-of-its-kind “Army Modernization Day” held on Capitol Hill earlier this month. Read more here .
The race to replace the Bradley heats up
Both XM30 contenders made their case at AUSA. General Dynamics Land Systems brought a one-eighth-scale model of the XM30 Wolf after delivering its first full-size prototype to the Army in August. Read more here .
American Rheinmetall delivered its first Lynx prototype in September, with seven more due by year’s end. Some troops have been able to see the vehicle and were able to hop inside and turn it on, a company official said, beginning a new era for Army combat vehicles. Read more here .
Infantry Squad Vehicle surge
GM Defense announced on Monday that the Army has expanded orders for the Infantry Squad Vehicle , or ISV, from the initial 649 to nearly 12,000.
The announcement means the service will be increasing its fleet of ISVs by roughly 1,750%.
The ISV and ISV-Heavy, which are modeled after GM’s Chevrolet Colorado ZR2 and Chevrolet Silverado HD 3500 ZR2, respectively, are designed to be adapted to changes on the battlefield rather than specific mission sets. Read more here .
Bell touts MV-75 Cheyenne II as combat game changer
The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.”
Although the Cheyenne ’s speed and weapons systems capabilities are expected to increase substantially, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software. Read more here .

Getting defensive
The PAC-3 Edge on display at AUSA. (Lockheed Martin)
New PAC-3 Edge interceptor aims for agility
The latest iteration of Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 family of missile interceptors is designed to bring extreme agility to bear against a diverse array of missile threats, Defense News learned.
Designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, the unveiling of the PAC-3 Edge at AUSA comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions. Read more here .
Anduril reveals family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles
Anduril announced a new family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles in an effort to create a more diverse range of defensive measures while building at scale.
Steelfin, a family of highly configurable, mass-producible, surface-to-air interceptor missiles, has been developed to deliver cost, volume and capability across a variety of threats, the company announced. Read more here .
BAE Systems unveils new layered air-defense system
BAE Systems on Monday unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones.
The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units. Read more here .
Powerus unveils fully autonomous drone interceptors
The South Carolina-based startup Powerus unveiled a fully autonomous version of its Guardian interceptor on Monday at AUSA.
Brett Velicovich, the company’s president and co-founder, said in an interview with Military Times that logical product upgrades have been key to the company’s success. He explained how the company’s growth, the evolution of its interceptors and rising U.S. military demand for drone-defense systems amid the war in Iran have converged. Read more here .
Northrop Grumman breaks out the big guns at AUSA
Amid the missiles and microelectronics, Northrop Grumman brought something more familiar to the floor: really big guns.
The company showed off Raid Hunter, a 50mm gun-based air defense system with AI targeting and proximity-fuzed rounds built for drone swarms and cruise missiles, and debuted a dual-feed M230 chain gun that lets crews switch between counter-drone and anti-armor ammo on the fly. Read more here .
Forterra partners with Hypercraft on autonomous vehicle for high-risk missions
Defense companies Forterra and Hypercraft have collaborated to produce a contested-environment-ready autonomous vehicle, which they showed off for the first time at AUSA.
Forterra installed its AutoDrive autonomy software platform that powers unmanned maneuverability onto Hypercraft’s Razorback ground vehicle, yielding a product that can withstand the punishing logistics of combat without putting soldiers at risk. Read more here .

Personnel
Participants in the U.S. Army's jungle school in Panama slog through mud during the course's culminating event, the Green Mile. (Eve Sampson/staff)
Back in the jungles of Panama
The U.S. Army has resumed a partnership with Panamanian forces, in which the country’s troops teach and attend the 18-day Jungle School.
As Panama’s troops have trained, lived — and in some cases, fought — in such environments, they are largely seen by U.S. personnel as the ultimate masters of the terrain. Read more here .
For soldiers of the 11th Airborne, ‘winter is always coming’
Survival in Alaska’s vast wilderness, where any hint of complacency can indeed kill, presents a colossal difficulty. Training service members to fight in these environs is an undertaking even more daunting.
For the soldiers of the U.S. Army’s 11th Airborne Division, this task rests, ultimately, on the shoulders of Maj. Gen. John Cogbill and the capable leaders he advises. Cogbill spoke to Military Times about what goes into warfighting in the far North. Read more here .
Generals propose larger-footprint, more frequent exercises in Korea
A month after President Donald Trump intervened to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing a desire not to upset his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, the commander of Army forces on the peninsula said he’d like to go bigger — both in exercise frequency and geographic scope.
Speaking at AUSA, Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there. Read more here .
‘Addicted to the Guard’: Generals call for a ‘traffic cop’ on governors’ demands
During a panel at AUSA, the message of National Guard leaders was clear: State demands of Guard troops are unsustainable — and they need to stop.
The effects are felt in equipment readiness and training, particularly as funding has not followed the deployment of units and their gear. Read more here .
Updates to testosterone screening
A quarter of troops measured below testosterone thresholds, a new study of Army personnel found, with similar results compared to the general U.S. population.
According to the research , 20% of male soldiers younger than 30 years had testosterone levels less than the threshold established by the American Urological Association of 300 nanograms per deciliter, or ng/dL. Roughly a third of service members — 32.8% — aged 30 and older fell below the threshold. Read more here .
‘Nobody’s losing pay’: Army Cyber Command head on new tech mastery program
The head of the U.S. Army’s digital defense wing on Monday reassured soldiers in the field that a new initiative aimed at enhancing cyberspace proficiency wouldn’t affect their pay.
The Cyber Mastery Incentive program debuted on Oct. 1, promising a new way of paying service members that rewards technology mastery and performance of demanding tasks. But reports emerged that the program wasn’t as financially enticing as advertised, with reductions in certain soldiers’ pay by up to $1,000 per month. Read more here .
