By Gavin van Marle
16 October 2026
Three months of declining container freight spot rates on the Asia-Europe trades were brought to an end this week when pricing reversed ahead of new FAK price hikes this month.
This week’s World Container Index (WCI) from Drewry saw the spot rate on its Shanghai-Rotterdam leg up 6% on the week before, at $3,522 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-Genoa route was up 7%, to $3,945 per 40ft.
Meanwhile, a range of new freight all kinds prices are due to be introduced by carriers on Monday, which forwarders said had been pushed back by a few days, and possibly explains this week’s rise.
The 19 October FAK rates range from: $4,200 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe and $4,600 on Asia-Mediterranean, as advised by Hapag-Lloyd; to CMA CGM’s $4,600 to North Europe and $4,700 to the Mediterranean; while MSC is looking for $4,500 per 40ft to both North and South Europe.
While this week’s WCI rise was enough to wipe out the past three weeks of Asia-Europe declines, forwarders told The Loadstar they expected rates to fall again.
“We did get FAK rate increases for the second half of October, and these were then pushed back to start 19 October, but I have received this morning downward revisions for those, almost back to the levels we saw in the first half of October,” one European forwarder told The Loadstar today.
“We’re not seeing any noticeable increase in demand – it’s all still a bit flat in that respect,” he added.
Meanwhile, another forwarder noted that, when carriers specified an end date to the FAK prices – 31 October by both MSC and CMA CGM – it usually suggested an expectation that rates were expected to soften.
“One useful indicator is when you see carriers place a time limit on the validity of their FAK pricing, as is the case now, because in my experience they don’t normally increase prices before that period expires,” the forwarder explained.
More concerning for forwarders and their shippers was the declining reliability of services, said Jon Charles, head of product at WiseTech, echoing many anecdotal reports The Loadstar recently received.
He said: “On Asia–Europe, the challenge we foresee is reliability rather than space. Only 9.9% of shipments arrived on time in September, and delays of eight days or more now account for almost half of volume, so building extra time into delivery commitments is essential.”
Meanwhile, MSC this week announced its Asia-North Europe Britannia service would be blanked in weeks 45 and 46, “due to ongoing market challenges”.
Source: Drewry
Spot rates on the transpacific trades diverged this week, with the WCI’s Shanghai-Los Angeles route up 3%, to $7,884 per 40ft, while its Shanghai-New York price continued a gradual descent that began three weeks ago.
This week it fell 1%, to $10,075 per 40ft, although Drewry noted that “strong US import demand continues to support transpacific rates”.
US west coast forwarder Freight Right said carriers had this week prioritised clearing backlogs that had built up during Golden Week, which made space for new bookings difficult to secure and propped up spot rates.
“Post-holiday backlogs are taking priority – containers rolled before or during the holiday are filling available slots, leaving fewer opportunities for new bookings,” it said.
“Vessel removals and service adjustments over recent months are keeping space tight – limited availability does not necessarily indicate stronger overall demand,” it added.

HondaJet Classic Jets Can Now Be Flown in Europe With APMG S Upgrades
13 photos
Photo: HondaJet
At the end of 2025, American plane maker Honda Aircraft Company announced an upgrade package for the relatively old HondaJet Classic aircraft lineup in a bid to give it modern capabilities, in line with the newer Elite S. This week, the upgrade solution, titled APMG S, got cleared for use in the European Union as well, following type validation from American and Mexican regulators.
APMG stands for Advanced Performance Modification Group S, and it’s an upgrade package meant to make the Classic jets, initially produced from 2015 to 2018, both safer to fly and better at their job, in line with present-day expectations.
For the Classic, that includes features the plane didn’t originally have, including upgraded avionics software, tweaked hardware, and faster processing speeds. On top of everything, the planes gain the ability to be upgraded further in the future as new technologies emerge.
APMG also brings to the table the Advanced Steering Augmentation System (ASAS) that, on the HondaJet Elite S, increases handling and crosswind capabilities, and an increase in maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 300 pounds (136 kg) - the total now stands at 10,900 pounds (4,944 kg).
Finally, new graphical weight and balance features are included in the mix, giving pilots the ability to quickly calculate takeoff and landing weights using loading and fuel data.
According to HondaJet, a plane running the APMG S package comes with improved performance numbers. The plane’s maximum speed is now 422 knots (486 mph/728 kph), the max cruise altitude it can reach is 43,000 feet (13,100 meters), while the range, when flying with four people on board and equipped with fuel reserves, is now 1,563 miles (2,517 km).
For HondaJet operators on the Old Continent, word of the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) clearing the upgrade package must feel like a blessing, but, in all fairness, though, I was kind of expecting HondaJet to give us an update on the new version of the airplane called Echelon.
First presented during the 2023 National Business Aviation Convention and Exhibition (NBAA-BACE) in Las Vegas, the newcomer is supposed to be the most advanced of its kind yet, with a pair of Williams International engines giving it the ability to fly at speeds of up to 833 mph (1,340 kph) and reach distances of up to 3,000 miles (4,828 km).
A perfect fit, then, to link Point Arena, California, to West Quoddy Head, Maine, the greatest distance between two mainland points in the U.S.. And that should make it the world's only transcontinental single-pilot light jet currently available.
We know the upcoming jet will be available in two configurations, serving different operator needs: one crew and ten passengers, or two crew and nine passengers. It’s likely the new aircraft will be chasing type certification in 2028.

By Charlotte Goldstone
16 October 2026
DHL Express has committed €300m in investment across Africa through to 2030, as the logistics group urges UK businesses to diversify supply chains and pursue opportunities in an area expected to become a major global growth engine by 2035.
Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, said the investment “reflected the company’s confidence in the continent’s long-term prospects”, amid shifting global trade relationships, geopolitical tensions, and changes to supply chains.
“We would not commit to €300m if we didn’t believe in the future of this continent,” he said today.
The announcement followed UK-Africa trade reaching approximately £52bn ($69bn) last year, according to figures cited by Mr Heymans. While modest compared with the UK’s overall trade, DHL executives argued that the relationship offered scope for expansion as businesses reassess traditional sourcing and export markets.
John Cornish, CEO of DHL Express UK, warned that British companies risked missing opportunities if they overlooked African markets while other economies strengthened their commercial relationships across the continent.
China’s expanding trade presence provided a key point of comparison, while the UK’s Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS) could help facilitate exports from eligible African countries, the executives said.
Mr Cornish said businesses should consider Africa both as a customer market and as a source of goods, rather than concentrating on established trading partners in Europe and the US.
“To UK companies, ignore this market at at the peril of your business,” he urged.
South Africa remains the UK’s largest trading partner on that continent, and Mr Heymans said UK imports from the country were worth approximately £7.5bn, with metals, agricultural products, and gold-related goods among the main categories.
Speakers also highlighted opportunities in energy, critical minerals, electric vehicles, healthcare, and life sciences. Indeed, Mr Heymans reported double-digit growth in DHL’s life sciences and healthcare business in the region, while engineering and manufacturing activity had declined.
However, infrastructure deficits, customs barriers, regulatory differences, and limited connectivity continued to complicate trade, Mr Heymans warned. He said only 12% of African cities were connected by at least one commercial flight a week, underscoring the challenges facing companies seeking to expand manufacturing and distribution.
DHL is looking to address some of these constraints through its existing network, which Mr Heymans said spanned every African country and territory. In sub-Saharan Africa, the company operates 12 dedicated aircraft, alongside road transport, facilities and other air connections.
The executives stressed that businesses should not approach Africa as a single market, given the differences in languages, legal systems, currencies, and trade regulations.

JERUSALEM — Israel is set to acquire 12 Apache “Echo” attack helicopters from Boeing, according to an Israeli ministry of defense announcement this week.
The deal secures the advanced variant of the helicopter, with scheduled delivery at the beginning of the next decade. It follows months of uncertainty surrounding the deal’s viability, caused by the Israeli government’s inability to finalize the pact despite multiple offer extensions granted by the Americans.
An agreement was previously stalled due to a dispute between the Israeli ministry of finance and the Israeli ministry of defense over funding sources. The ministry of finance demanded budget adjustments and a defined funding source, while the defense establishment pressed to approve the procurement as “urgent,” regardless of general budget discussions.
This gridlock persisted even as the U.S. granted Israel several extensions, culminating in a deadline of Oct. 7, 2026. After missing this original window, concerns arose in Israel that Boeing’s production slot would be routed to other international customers, leading to delivery delays and price increases.
In a last-minute move, Israeli defense officials reached out to their U.S. counterparts and requested another extension. The Americans agreed and opened what Israeli officials conveyed to the press here as a “final window” on the condition that the deal be signed immediately. This prompted an urgent Israeli Cabinet phone vote on Wednesday, which approved the necessary budgetary source at the expense of another long-term, non-defense national program, and made the signing of the deal possible at the same day.
The AH-64E Apache “Echo” is a twin-engine, tandem-seat attack helicopter. The aircraft’s integrated weapon and targeting suite accommodates a payload of up to 16 Hellfire missiles, 76 2.75-inch rockets, and an M230-series 30mm automatic chain gun supplied with up to 1,200 rounds of ammunition.
The platform incorporates digital network connectivity via Link 16, manned-unmanned teaming capabilities for drone control, and a modular open systems approach designed to allow the integration of hardware and software modifications.

A California jury has awarded nearly $9.4 million to a medical supply distributor after finding that a Wyoming-based logistics broker and its managing member made fraudulent representations that led to a failed $9.5 million shipment of medical gloves.
The Los Angeles County Superior Court jury found Oak Sourcing & Logistics LLC and Matthew John Sandvig liable for intentional misrepresentation in a dispute with Ashtel Studios Inc., a California company that imported nitrile examination gloves during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Oct. 9 verdict awarded Ashtel $9.397 million in economic damages, including $6.43 million in out-of-pocket expenditures and nearly $2.97 million in other economic losses.
The dispute centered on Oak Sourcing’s representations about its financial resources, customer contracts and ability to purchase millions of boxes of medical gloves.
According to Ashtel’s original complaint, Sandvig told company executives in March 2021 that Oak Sourcing had an $800 million personal protective equipment contract, long-term supply commitments with hospitals and access to substantial financing.
Those representations helped persuade Ashtel to enter into two large glove transactions totaling $14.7 million, according to the complaint.
Two shipments, one unpaid order
The companies’ first transaction, dated July 2, 2021, involved 500,000 boxes of nitrile gloves valued at $5.2 million.
Ashtel imported the gloves from China through the Port of Long Beach in 14 shipping containers. The products were subsequently transported to the company’s warehouse in Ontario, California.
Oak Sourcing eventually paid for the first shipment in August 2021, approximately three weeks after its arrival, although Ashtel alleged that certain transportation and warehousing expenses remained unpaid.
A second purchase order, dated July 7, 2021, called for 1 million boxes of nitrile examination gloves at $9.50 per box, totaling $9.5 million.
The second shipment arrived in 27 containers, but Oak Sourcing allegedly failed to complete payment or take possession of the merchandise.
Ashtel alleged that the broker repeatedly delayed inspections, requested additional shipping documentation and indicated that payment would follow receipt of funds from its downstream customer.
The company later learned that Oak Sourcing’s purported end customer was another intermediary rather than a hospital or other direct purchaser, according to the complaint.
Ashtel said it incurred additional drayage, warehousing and storage expenses while attempting to resolve the transaction and eventually resold the gloves to reduce its losses.
The two purchase orders involved a combined 1.5 million boxes of gloves transported in 41 ocean shipping containers.
Jury finds intentional misrepresentation
The jury concluded that both Oak Sourcing and Sandvig made false representations, knew those statements were false or acted recklessly regarding their truth, and intended Ashtel to rely on them.
Jurors also found that Ashtel reasonably relied on those representations and suffered financial harm as a result.
In addition to the $9.397 million fraud award, the jury found that Oak Sourcing owed Ashtel $4,272,252 on an open book account claim.
That finding represents a separate legal claim, and the amount should not be added to the fraud award without determining how the court will address overlapping damages in its final judgment.
The jury also rejected Oak Sourcing’s counterclaims against Ashtel, including allegations of intentional and negligent misrepresentation, concealment and breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
Jurors further determined that Sandvig engaged in conduct involving malice, oppression or fraud, potentially exposing the defendants to punitive damages.
However, Ashtel agreed to forgo punitive damages in exchange for the defendants waiving their rights to challenge the judgment through post-trial motions, appeals or other proceedings, according to Eugene Rome, founding partner of Rome LLP, which represented Ashtel.
Rome clarified that the agreement was not an additional monetary settlement.
The jury’s findings underscore the distinction between a failed commercial transaction and fraud, Rome said.
“A fraud verdict is a finding that the representations about the company and the volume of business it had were knowingly false when they were made,” Rome said in an Oct. 13 statement . “That goes well beyond a breach of contract.”
The litigation began in March 2022, when Ashtel filed a federal lawsuit against Sandvig, Oak Sourcing and Oak Insurance Group LLC in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.
The defendants moved to dismiss the federal action for lack of jurisdiction. Ashtel subsequently voluntarily dismissed the case without prejudice, and a federal judge closed the proceeding in May 2022 without ruling on the merits.
The dispute continued in Los Angeles County Superior Court, where Judge Nicole M. Heeseman presided over the jury trial.
Although the jury has returned its verdict, the case has not been fully resolved.
Rome told FreightWaves that Ashtel intends to submit a proposed judgment for the court’s approval.
A separate bench trial concerning alter ego allegations involving Oak Insurance Group will also proceed at a future date, he said.
Those allegations concern whether the related business entities should be treated as legally separate for purposes of liability. No finding against Oak Insurance Group is established by the jury verdict.
Rome said the case illustrates the risks of relying on a counterparty’s representations when entering large commercial transactions.
“While large transactions create the prospects of substantial profits, they equally entail traps for the unwary,” Rome told FreightWaves.
Oak Sourcing & Logistics is identified in the litigation as a Wyoming-based intermediary in medical supply transactions. The available court records do not establish that it operated as a federally licensed freight broker .
FreightWaves attorneys representing Oak Sourcing & Logistics. No responses had been received as of publication.
Why it matters: The verdict highlights the financial risks facing suppliers and logistics intermediaries when major transactions rely on misleading claims about customer contracts and purchasing capacity.

Estuary Biotherapeutics is ready to sail the seas, with $103 million in financing and two lead gene therapy programs for kidney disease.
The biotech emerged from stealth on Friday , announcing a $93 million series A and an earlier $10 million seed financing. Co-founder Wayne Sackett, previously of MyoKardia, will serve as CEO.
Estuary is aiming to tackle the root cause of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), which is the most common genetic form of end-stage kidney disease worldwide. The disease causes fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys which gradually leads to a decline in function.
The company’s pipeline is built around the science of Stefan Somlo and Michael Caplan at the Yale School of Medicine. The scientists demonstrated that restoring the expression of polycystin in kidneys that have evidence of cystic disease can reverse the condition in mice.

By Alex Lennane
16 October 2026
Freight forwarders must tackle unbilled charges, manual rework, and unreliable data before expecting AI to protect their margins, according to Metro Shipping and Portcast.
Speaking on The Loadstar Podcast , Ian Powell, tech and solutions director at Metro, said profitability could be eroded by incorrect buy and sell rates, costs not passed on to customers, and repeated administrative work.
“If we’re constantly reworking activity, if we’re raising credits against jobs, re-invoicing jobs, that’s not optimal for us from an operating cost point of view,” he said.
Emma Crumpton, enterprise solutions director at freight intelligence platform Portcast, highlighted detention and demurrage as a particularly complex source of margin erosion.
Different free-time allowances, charging milestones, and contractual terms make managing charges difficult at scale. Forwarders may also absorb costs to protect customer relationships.
“When I think about detention and demurrage, it’s a complexity issue,” she said.
Technology could help identify approaching free-time deadlines and ensure charges were correctly recorded and billed. But both guests stressed that automation depended on reliable data and understanding the task.
Mr Powell said Metro’s adoption of airfreight tracking technology included a three-month pilot to integrate systems and resolve problems. Forwarders should identify the root causes of losses, with some problems addressable through process changes.
“You don’t need to apply AI for the sake of it,” added Ms Crumpton.
That echoed Australian forwarder Neolink’s experience. In an earlier interview with The Loadstar , Sean Crook said around half its shipment workflow incorporated automation.
“Automation, to be honest, has probably been even bigger for us than AI,” he said.
Mr Crook said Neolink’s staff were handling 80% to 90% more shipment volume than three years earlier, without an increase in staff numbers. He attributed the gains to both technology and a business model that gives customers a single contact responsible for the relationship from start to finish, reducing departmental handovers.
Its approach also relies on obtaining purchase-order information early enough to plan shipments, rather than waiting until goods are ready. Mr Crook said receiving orders two or more weeks in advance helped the forwarder make earlier bookings and choose services suited to customers’ actual inventory requirements, avoiding unnecessary premiums for speed they did not need.
Meanwhile, The Loadstar’s State of AI in Supply Chain 2026 report found 48.7% of respondents cited integration with existing systems as a major barrier to scaling AI; while 53.8% identified insufficient in-house AI expertise and change-management capability.
Looking ahead, the podcast guests saw opportunities to turn shipment data into practical insights, while retaining human oversight of decisions affecting customers and profitability.

Waymo is bringing its robotaxis to Canada, and Toronto is first. Its cars will start driving the city’s streets in the coming days, and the company wants its first public riders on board in 2028.
That makes Toronto Waymo’s fourth announced market outside the US, after London, Tokyo, and Singapore. But there’s a catch: Ontario doesn’t have rules for a commercial driverless service yet.
Mapping first, riders in 2028
Waymo announced the expansion on its blog today. As in every new city, its cars will start out manually driven. Specialists behind the wheel will build high-definition maps and validate the software on Toronto streets before anything runs without a human.
For operations, Waymo is bringing in Element Fleet Management, which is headquartered in Toronto, to run end-to-end fleet management. It also pointed to two Canadian companies already in its corner: the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, a long-term investor, and Magna International, its manufacturing partner.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana called Canada “an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey.”
Waymo also says it and its partners will create “hundreds of roles” over time in fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and operations. That line is there for a reason. In April, Mayor Olivia Chow’s office told the Toronto Star it wouldn’t support Waymo if the service cost jobs, and that the company “must demonstrate this will not happen.”
Ontario’s rules run out before Waymo’s launch
Waymo’s post doesn’t mention a single permit or approval.
Ontario has allowed automated vehicle testing since 2016 under a pilot regulation, O. Reg. 306/15, and added driverless testing in 2019. According to Ontario’s e-Laws database , that regulation is revoked on October 13, 2027, months before Waymo wants to carry riders, and the province hasn’t said what replaces it.
It’s also a testing framework, not a ride-hailing licence. Transport Canada told Canadian Affairs last week that self-driving vehicles on public roads are limited to “temporary pilot projects” run by the provinces. So Waymo’s 2028 date depends on Doug Ford’s government writing rules that don’t exist today.
The safety case Waymo is bringing
Waymo’s pitch rests on its US record. The company says it has driven more than 400 million fully autonomous kilometres (roughly 250 million miles) and that its vehicles were involved in 95% fewer crashes causing serious injury or worse than human drivers in the cities where it operates.
As we reported last month , Waymo now claims its cars have prevented 841 injuries. It’s carrying more than 500,000 paid rides a week across over a dozen US metros, and it went driverless in Las Vegas this summer with Denver, San Diego, and Tampa following.
Denver matters here. It’s Waymo’s first real snow city, and Toronto’s winters, with slush, road salt, and freezing rain coating sensors for months, are exactly what the long manual-driving phase is meant to test. Waymo calls its system “all-weather.” Toronto will check that claim.
Compare that to Tesla. Its “Robotaxi” service runs in seven US cities, Tesla still doesn’t disclose how many cars operate without a safety monitor, and the fleet has been barely running for much of the year. Tesla hasn’t put a date on carrying riders in a single Canadian city.
Electrek’s Take
This is the right way to enter a new country. Waymo isn’t promising driverless rides next month. It’s giving itself more than two years and at least two Toronto winters of data before anyone pays for a ride, which is exactly how it built a US service that now does half a million paid trips a week.
Queen’s Park and City Hall might give them trouble. Ontario’s only legal framework for these cars expires next October, there’s no path yet from a testing permit to a paid service, and Toronto’s mayor has already made jobs the condition for her support. Waymo clearly read that, which is why Element and “hundreds of roles” are front and center in its announcement.
I think Waymo gets there, but 2028 is Ontario’s deadline to hit as much as Waymo’s. If the province lets the pilot lapse without a commercial framework, Canada’s biggest city ends up watching London and Tokyo get robotaxis first.
And for those of us in Montreal: Quebec, your move.

DHL Group said it plans to invest more than $447 million in logistics infrastructure, freight services and technology in Central and Eastern Europe by 2030 because the region is home to a growing number of innovative, high-growth companies that need supply chain, international transportation and distribution services.
DHL ( XETRA: DHL ) is focusing investment in sectors and geographic regions that offer high-growth opportunities, with the goal of increasing revenue by 50% between 2023 and 2030. Last year, DHL Group said it would invest more than $570 million to expand capacity and capabilities in the Middle East.
The express freight company said it has added Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania to its 2030 strategic growth plan because the region is playing an increasingly important role in production and trade, while also being a large consumption market. The four countries are increasingly attracting European manufacturers and distributors, and foreign companies seeking closer proximity to the European consumer market as part of a growing nearshoring trend.
Why It Matters: DHL is one of the largest third-party logistics providers in the world.
The investment program spans most business groups, supporting capacity expansion in warehousing, ground freight transportation, supply chain control towers and international express services, including the planned construction of a new DHL Express air freight express terminal in Katowice, DHL said in a news release last week.
“Central and Eastern Europe is becoming increasingly important for global trade flows and supply chain networks. Poland, in particular, is developing into one of Europe’s most dynamic logistics and manufacturing hubs,” said John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express. “As customers strive for greater resilience and flexibility, they need logistics partners who can seamlessly connect production, inventory, and markets across borders. With these investments, we are expanding the infrastructure and international connectivity required to support the growth ambitions of the dynamic companies driving the economic development of this region.”
Poland grows as major trade hub
Poland has become a regional economic power over the past 30 years, with merchandise trade growing more than two times faster than global trade and 2.7 times faster than trade within the European Union over the past decade, according to the DHL Globalization Tracker published this month. The report, written in conjunction with New York University’s Stern School of Business, forecasts Poland’s goods trade will grow 28% faster than global trade and 91% faster than EU trade over the next three years.
The analysis also shows an increasing diversification of Poland’s trade relations. While Germany remains an important trading partner and the majority of Polish trade takes place within the European Union, trade with both the United States and China has increased significantly over the past 10 years.
“Central and Eastern Europe is consolidating its role as a strategic location for production, distribution, and regional fulfillment activities, particularly for companies seeking closer proximity to the European market,” said Hendrik Venter, CEO of DHL Supply Chain.
The contract logistics unit, for example, recently entered the Romanian market through an expanded partnership with Polish retailer Pepco.
DHL said Poland will continue to play a central role in its growth ambitions for the region. DHL Group has already invested significantly in the Polish market in recent years. In 2024, DHL opened a $201 million international logistics centre in Poznań, one of the largest logistics investments in the company’s history in Poland. The site supports several DHL business units, including DHL eCommerce, DHL Freight, and Post & Parcel Germany, and also serves as a key logistics hub connecting Poland with European and global markets.
DHL eCommerce operates a significant network of fulfillment centers, parcel lockers and pickup points in Poland in support of e-commerce marketplaces.
Poland is among DHL Group’s 10 largest markets worldwide in terms of the number of employees, with more than 10,000 people working there.
More warehouse capacity in Germany
DHL Group also continues to invest in Germany, where the company is headquartered.
DHL Express last week officially opened a new station in Cologne-Marsdorf, significantly expanding its capacity in the region.The 215,000-square foot site features three Pick-up and Delivery bays with 78 loading and unloading bays, a warehouse area with 35 bays of its own, and a modern sortation system capable of processing up to 6,000 domestic and international parcels.
DHL Express is midway through construction of a new sort station in eastern Germany. (Photo: DHL)
The site includes 78 charging points for electric vehicles.
DHL also said it is on track to complete a new 315,000-square foot logistics center outside Jena, Germany, by March.
Jena is a high-tech industrial city in the eastern German state of Thuringia. DHL said the warehouse will offer logistics services for growing businesses in high-tech manufacturing, semiconductors, healthcare and battery technology. One of DHL Supply Chain’s key customers in the area is Zeiss, a leading manufacturer of eyeglass lenses, camera and cinematic lenses, and binoculars.

1970 Plymouth Satellite Springs Back to Life After 36 Years at a Farm; Too Many Doors?
12 photos
Photo: Rocket Restorations/YouTube
In 1965, Plymouth redesigned its intermediate car lineup for the first time. While the Belvedere remained in production, the Savoy was discontinued, while the Fury nameplate was returned to the full-size market. To replace the latter, Plymouth introduced the Satellite.
A more upscale version of the Belvedere, the original Satellite was also a more performance-oriented Mopar. It came standard with a V8 engine, and it was restricted to two-door body styles (hardtop and convertible). It was Plymouth's range-topping intermediate until 1967, when the company debuted the GTX.
With the latter taking over premium muscle car duties, the Satellite was overhauled for the 1968 model year, gaining additional body styles. Much like the cheaper Belvedere, the B-body was also offered in four-door sedan and station wagon iterations. Plymouth retained this lineup until the Satellite was discontinued in 1974.
Although it's overshadowed by the GTX and Road Runner , the Satellite gets a bit of love from classic car collectors, particularly when equipped with the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8. These cars are also quite rare. The 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) V8 models are also somewhat sought-after in two-door body configurations.
Other engines and body styles? Well, these cars are far from desirable, especially if they have four doors. Moreover, most of them are actually rotting away in junkyards and barns, with no hope of getting back on the road. And that's precisely why you need to see this 1970 Satellite.
Far from surprising for a four-door sedan, this Plymouth was parked decades ago. It retired in 1990 and spent the next few decades at a farm, without a single sip of gasoline. But unlike many of its siblings, it was kept safe from the elements, so it soldiered on without significant rust issues. Its interior was infested by rodents, but the body is in surprisingly good condition after all these years.
Also unlike most of its siblings, this Satellite got a second chance at life. YouTube's "Rocket Restoration" found it by accident on Facebook Marketplace and decided to send a friend and bid for it at a far auction. He got it for "a reasonable price," brought it back home, and got it running again with help from his buddy at YouTube's "Dead Dodge Garage."
The Satellite was born with the 318-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) V8 engine, which was the standard powerplant in 1970. The original owner opted for the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic, which means that this Mopar sports a rather common drivetrain.
Is it worth reviving to the point it becomes road-worthy? Well, it may become a nice car once that dreadful interior is cleaned up (it sure looks like it smells terrible in there). However, I can't see this Satellite getting a full restoration. It's just not worth it relative to its current market value.
And as our host puts it, some of its body panels fit other more desirable Mopars, and selling them separately would bring more bucks. Unfortunately, this Satellite may end up being dismantled. It's a shame, but that's how the cookie crumbles sometimes.

This Sailing Catamaran Is Built for Long-Range Ocean Voyages and Luxury Living
15 photos
Photo: JFA Yachts
French shipyard JFA Yachts has just announced the launch of a new sailing catamaran for bluewater cruising. Called the Long Island 87, the new multi-hull leisure vessel was developed for long-distance voyages, combining sailing performance with spacious living areas and the autonomy needed for extended cruising.
Over the last two decades, catamarans have seen a remarkable evolution, revolutionizing the maritime world with their unique designs that ensure a level of stability, comfort, and spaciousness you can not find in monohull vessels. While power catamarans have attracted owners looking for exhilarating speed and the freedom to explore far-flung destinations, sailing catamarans have found a devoted following among those seeking serene, unhurried journeys and a harmonious connection with the sea.
The Long Island 87 is a magnificent vessel that belongs to the latter category. Sold in October 2023, the 86-foot (26.2-meter) multihull was built for an owner who plans to travel the globe with their family and offers them a symphony of freedom, comfort, and reliability, with the right balance between performance under sail and functional living spaces.
The new catamaran is part of the shipyard’s Long Island range, which also includes the smaller Long Island 85 and the larger Long Island 100, and builds on the experience gained from these previous models in the series. According to JFA Yachts, the first two Long Island 85 cats have completed extensive voyages to remote destinations, including Antarctica and Greenland, as well as routes across the Pacific and the Baltic Sea.
Photo: JFA Yachts Developed as part of a 15-year collaboration between JFA Yachts and Marc Lombard Yacht Design Group, this new model preserves many of the proven design features seen on the previous models, while also introducing new ones. As such, it is built with an aluminum hull combined with a composite deck and superstructure, a construction that helps keep displacement low without compromising strength and performance.
According to the French shipyard, the vessel has about 30% less displacement than comparable models on the market, allowing for higher average speeds and lower fuel consumption.
The superstructure, however, features more modern lines, and one of the yacht’s defining features is the expansive flybridge. This elevated upper deck is fitted with not one but two helm stations and is configured as a full-fledged living space with a covered bar area and a spacious, inviting lounge with multiple seating options. It also benefits from panoramic views of the surrounding ocean, and its roof is covered with solar panels.
The Long Island 87 also introduces a new interior layout to the line. With a beam of 39 feet (11.8 meters), the vessel offers generous living quarters, with enough room for both private relaxation and socializing. There are 1,330 square feet (124 square meters) of living space, and the updated layout is designed to accommodate up to ten guests and four crew members.
Photo: JFA Yachts The owner’s suite stretches across the full width of the main deck . It offers 180-degree views of the sea and benefits from direct access to the foredeck. The port hull houses a children’s cabin with four berths and an aft guest cabin, while the starboard hull includes another guest cabin and the crew quarters.
The main deck is also home to a cockpit and the interior salon, with a lounge on the port side and a dining area to starboard. Thanks to large windows and a glass door, the convivial spaces flow seamlessly into the aft deck, extending the living spaces outdoors. Here, owners will be able to enjoy a sunbathing area and a swim platform that can also fit a 16-foot (4.9-meter) tender.
Photo: JFA Yachts The sailing catamaran ’s interiors will be completely bespoke to reflect the owners’ preferences and tastes. Darnet Design will bring their vision to life.
“We are very excited to launch this Long Island 87’ project,” says the future owner. “We found this yacht to be the perfect balance between performance under sail and functional living spaces. The Long Island 87’ is the optimal proven blue water sailing catamaran available in the market today and well suited for our specific mission, to circumnavigate the globe with our family of four in unparalleled comfort, safety, and luxury.”

2027 Kawasaki KLE500 Lands with a Smarter Way to (Not) Use the Clutch
13 photos
Photo: Kawasaki
It’s been exactly a year since Japanese bike maker Kawasaki brought back the KLE500 dual-purpose motorcycle, and things are going so well that the company has now announced a new version is joining the range for the 2027 model year.
Until now, the revived KLE500 was a pretty small family, with only two models on the table: the standard and SE. Now, the SE Smartride variant is joining the party, bringing along a smarter way of (not) using the clutch.
Kawasaki calls it the Smartride, basically a self-engaging clutch system that works using a mechanical centrifugal clutch fitted inside a conventional assembly. Doing things this way is first and foremost supposed to reduce the need to use the clutch in high-intensity moments such as stop-and-go urban riding.
Then, it removes the need for delicate half-clutch control when pulling away from a stop, effectively taking clutch lever operation out of the equation. Naturally, normal shifting of gears with the use of the clutch is still on the table when riding.
Other than the fitting of the Smartride tech on this model for the first time, the KLE500 is still new enough to continue unchanged mechanically. That means we’re still dealing with a high-tensile steel trellis frame holding a fuel-injected 451cc parallel-twin engine.
The motorcycle rides on spoked wheels sized 21 inches at the front and 17 inches at the rear, which are supported by a KYB 43 mm inverted front fork with 210 mm of travel and a Uni-Trak rear system with 200 mm of travel. Stopping power is supplied by disc brakes with selectable ABS . For the new model year, Kawasaki is adding tubeless tires to the mix.
The bike’s design continues to be inspired by the worlds of rallying and motocross, and that means it also includes a skid plate and a tall front cowl for protection. There is also a windscreen on deck with three adjustable levels, and a fuel tank capable of holding 4.2 gallons (almost 16 liters).
The addition of the Smartride tech is, for now at least, limited to the European market. Over in the U.S., the two-wheeler continues to soldier on in its 2026 model year incarnation, with pricing set at $6,599 for the standard two-wheeler and $7,499 for the SE.
This one, short for Special Edition, adds a taller windshield, metal-reinforced hand guards, a larger skid plate, and LED lights. The LCD instrumentation on the standard is replaced by a 4.3-inch TFT screen. The color choices remain the same as before.
The Europeans are also treated to Edition machines in three distinct versions: Rally (Akrapovic titanium exhaust, radiator cover, and low passenger seat), Adventure Tourer (engine guard and a pair of two-liter panniers), and Top Case, carrying, as the name says, a top case.

J.B. Hunt Transport Services’ third quarter may prove to be a speed bump on the road to recovery. The company previously flagged significant cost pressures, some growth-related, heading into the Thursday print. To meet demand, some of its business units offered sign-on bonuses and increase driver recruitment spending. Some costs appear transitory, while others may linger through the end of the year.
J.B. Hunt ( NASDAQ: JBHT ) reported third-quarter revenue of $3.68 billion, which was 20% higher year over year and ahead of the $3.59 billion consensus estimate. Earnings per share of $1.82 were 6 cents higher y/y and 1 cent above analysts’ lowered expectations. (A higher tax rate was a 4-cent EPS headwind in the period, partially offset by a 2-cent decline in net interest expense.)
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Consolidated
The company identified roughly $45 million in costs at an investor conference in mid-September. A sharp spike in diesel prices, driver hiring costs and elevated cargo claims forced the company to guide to a 5% to 10% sequential EPS decline in the third quarter (implying $1.77 at the midpoint of the range). The actual impact from the items totaled over $50 million in the period.
However, management told analysts on a Thursday evening call that “everything [is] playing out like a normal cycle,” noting it is common to incur incremental costs ahead of higher pricing and revenue.
“Any time that we see this pressure happening from a driver environment, [it] typically yields a much better pricing environment for the next bid season ,” said President and CEO Shelley Simpson.
The brunt of the cost-price mismatch likely occurred in August and September, and should fade as the magnitude of the cost pressure eases and recent contractual rate wins bleed through to results. It said office headcount was down 4.5% y/y in the period, as driver count increased 3.5%.
Fuel surcharges operate on a one-week lag. Diesel prices were up sequentially in nine of the 13 weeks of the third quarter. By month, retail diesel prices dipped 1% sequentially in July, but increased 10% sequentially in August and another 15% in September. The near-term headwind will become an earnings tailwind when prices revert.
The third quarter marked a fifth straight quarter of y/y improvement in operating income and EPS. The company’s earnings turnaround started in the 2025 third quarter, well ahead of peers.
Intermodal can exit 2027 operating within margin target range
Intermodal revenue increased 20% y/y to $1.83 billion as loads were up 8.5% and revenue per load increased 11%.
The period was up against an easier volume comparison to a year ago (-1%). By month, shipments grew y/y by 9% in July, 8% in August and 9% in September. Shipments increased 18% y/y in the East and 1% in the transcontinental network. Total intermodal carloads were up 6% y/y on the U.S. Class I railroads in the period (North American container moves were up 5% y/y).
Excluding fuel, revenue per load was up just 2% y/y. However, a 3% decline in length of haul, due to the mix shift to the East, was a modest headwind to yield metric. Management said it captured low-single-digit contractual rate increase in the 2026 bid season, which ended last month.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Intermodal
Sonar data shows the mode is currently 31% cheaper than truck, which is notably higher than the typical 10% to 15% discount carried in the East (approximately 25% in the West). Elevated truckload rates and record diesel prices remain ample tailwinds for road-to-rail conversion.
SONAR: Intermodal Contract Savings Index (IMCSI.USA). The IMCSI shows the savings percentage between domestic intermodal contract rate per mile and truckload contract rate per mile. The comparison includes fuel surcharges. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
Chart: (ORAILDOML.USA). The daily volume of intermodal containers moving in the United States, Canada and Mexico. The index is a 7-day moving average using the date that containers were in-gated at a point of origin. Intermodal trailers (trailer-on-flatcar) are excluded.
The unit booked a 91.9% operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 15 basis points worse y/y. Higher costs (driver personnel, equipment and employee benefits) led to an 11% increase in cost per load, offsetting the increase in yield.
The company’s container fleet was 92.1% utilized in the quarter, 170 bps better than in the second quarter and well ahead of the 83.6% utilization rate in the 2025 third quarter. However, average loads per container were down 1% y/y in the period, possibly due to a modest deterioration in rail service.
Improved rates and continued cost management could restore margins to the company’s long-term target range of 10% to 12% by the end of next year, management said.
Dedicated a Q3 cost victim
The dedicated unit’s OR deteriorated 360 bps y/y to 91.5%.
Revenue increased 11% y/y to $960 million as revenue per truck per week increased 10% and average trucks in service were up 1%. Revenue per truck was up just 3% excluding fuel. J.B. Hunt sold service on 425 trucks in the quarter (970 trucks year-to-date), but its pipeline remains at an all-time high.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Dedicated
Higher driver costs, group medical claims, insurance premiums and new account startup costs were among the headwinds in the quarter. It also incurred an elevated level of startup costs at new accounts. Average trailers in service increased 11% y/y even though loads grew just 3%.
It said it can revisit customer contracts and recoup incremental costs, like higher driver costs, before the annual rollover.
Brokerage books another profit
After 13 quarters operating in the red, the brokerage unit booked a second straight operating profit.
Revenue increased 57% y/y as loads grew 22% and revenue per load jumped 29% (inclusive of fuel). A 14.3% gross margin was 70 bps lower y/y but 180 bps better than the second quarter . Purchased transportation costs (spot rates) cooled following the Fourth of July. Loads per employee fell 5% y/y but gross profit per employee increased 17%. Headcount was 28% higher y/y.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Brokerage
The company’s asset-light TL unit returned to profit after a modest second-quarter loss. The $7-million operating profit was driven by a 29% y/y increase in revenue per load (excluding fuel) and a 4% increase in trailer utilization (loads per average trailer). The operating income result was roughly flat y/y.
Table: J.B. Hunt’s key performance indicators – Final Mile & Truckload
Shares of JBHT were down 3% in pre-market trading on Friday. The stock fell 14% from its mid-September earnings update to the Thursday close.
Why it matters? J.B. Hunt’s quarterly results serve as a bellwether for the intermodal, trucking and logistics industries. The company’s third quarter was a modest slowdown after four quarters of strong recovery. However, some of the incremental costs that plagued the period were likely transitory in nature.

By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
16 October 2026
Container lines, sensing a gradual slowdown in Indian westbound volumes, are revisiting their surcharges and penalties, indicating a hot market may be turning decidedly cooler.
The liners had been increasingly rolling booking cancellation and container no-show fees into their freight bills in recent months to maximise profitability from booming demand.
Now, according to industry sources, Hapag-Lloyd, for one, has revised its cancellation fee drastically for Indian customers to $100 per container, from the $300 in force since late July.
The German carrier reportedly had the highest such charge among the major carriers, sparking concerns for Indian exporters as they scrambled for vessel space.
And the carrier had previously announced a $300 per box “container rollover fee” to be applied when a booking was rolled within 10 days of the original vessel departure. This month’s reduction seems to cover both fees.
One forwarder told The Loadstar: “The market is shifting to the shippers’ side. There is now no room for carriers to recover all kinds of surcharges, as they want.”
The disruption in the Middle East had prompted a wave of hefty emergency surcharges by all carriers, sparking pushback and questions from various maritime regulatory authorities across their markets, including in India. In early March, the Directorate of General of Shipping warned the lines against “indulging in predatory or opportunistic pricing”.
Meanwhile, cargo bookings across westbound trades from India have dropped in recent days, signalling the beginning of a market downturn after a strong peak season. As a result, ocean rates, ex-India to Europe and the US, are trending down, with expectations that the recent elevated levels will halve over the next few weeks.
Indeed, Hapag-Lloyd yesterday advised forwarders it had revised spot rates for bookings on the 8,000 teu Tucapel , one of the vessels deployed on its TPI service between India (leaving JNPA on 24 October) and the US east coast, to $8,000 per 40ft – a reduction of around $1,500.
India’s exports have had an upbeat run over the past few months, showing high double-digit growth, according to government data; by value, surging 23% year on year last month, continuing the demand rally seen in prior months.
The recent peak season has also begun to show up in Container Trade Statistics (CTS) data, which now includes August, with all-in rates on the India/Middle East-North America trade showing sharp year-on-year growth…
Source: Container Trades Statistics
… while India-Europe rates have been on a longer rally since March, overcoming a mid-year wobble.
Source: Container Trades Statistics
“September’s strong export growth is an encouraging affirmation of India’s competitiveness in a challenging global trading environment,” said SC Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “Our exporters continue to respond to uncertainty with agility, strengthening their presence across markets and product categories.”
That momentum was also reflected in container volumes handled at the major Indian ports: JNPA saw record throughput of some 835,000 teu last month, up from 649,000 teu in September 2025.

City Therapeutics will join a slew of biotechs that have entered the public markets this year, with a $200 million raise that landed above expectations.
City Therapeutics, the RNA interference biotech developing therapies for thromboembolic diseases, has pulled off an upsized IPO, raising $200 million that will be split across its pipeline.
The company will begin trading on the Nasdaq Friday under the ticker CTY, after offering over 11 million shares at $18 apiece, according to the Thursday press release . Originally, City had targeted a sale of about 9.7 million shares for $158.3 million but has exceeded that, and another 1.6 million shares are being offered to the underwriters.
City will join a bustling group of biotechs that have joined the Nasdaq this year, including Aktis Oncology, Generate:Biomedicines and ADARx Pharmaceuticals. City’s $200 million raise falls in the middle of the pack, with a record high achieved this year by Parabilis Medicines’ $670 million IPO in June.

Most supply chain leaders say their employees are unprepared to use AI, according to a new report from the Association for Supply Chain Management ( ASCM ) and the Digital Supply Chain Institute ( DSCI ). The study found that 83% of respondents say their workers aren’t ready to use AI effectively, even as their companies plan to make it part of everyday work.
What’s Related
The joint study, The People Paradox in Supply Chain AI Integration , found that 91% of organizations plan to use AI to help human workers, while just 7% expect it to directly replace them.
Researchers collected 144 survey responses and used 107 for detailed analysis. Respondents included managers, directors, executives, and staff, with about 62% based in North America.
“AI adoption in supply chain is more about people than it is technology ,” said ASCM CEO Abe Eshkenazi. “The organizations making real progress treat workforce readiness as part of the technology investment, not an afterthought. They learn by doing, bring managers into the process early, and build trust one function at a time.”
RELATED STORIES: Half of Supply Chain Leaders Lack Talent to Run AI Tools | Why So Few Supply Chains Have Fully Embraced AI
Managers know about AI projects but often aren’t involved
The report found that half of directors, 51% of managers, and 70% of staff knew about their organizations’ AI initiatives without actively participating. Another 20% of staff reported no involvement at all.
Workforce skills and resources tied to an unclear business case or return on investment were the most frequently cited barriers, each at 33%. Poor data quality followed at 25%, while change management and governance or compliance risks each drew 21%.
Companies that described their workforce as prepared reported a 71% AI project success rate, compared with 28% among unprepared organizations. The prepared group had used AI across an average of six supply chain functions, while roughly 64% of unprepared organizations remained in planning or pilot stages.
Planning leads, but AI rarely makes decisions on its own
Across 13 supply chain functions, average AI adoption scored 1.94 on a five-point scale. A score of one meant no AI use, while five meant AI could act without human review.
Demand planning led at 2.28, followed by supply and inventory planning at 2.12. Reverse logistics ranked last at 1.59, and 55% of respondents described their AI projects as somewhat successful.
The report recommends involving directors and managers early in tool selection and work process design. It also calls for starting with a manageable project with clean data, a responsible owner and measurable results.
“With tariff shifts, demand shocks and geopolitical disruption , the advantage will go to companies that can sense and re-plan fastest. That makes AI readiness a management challenge first and a technology challenge second,” said Marko Kovacevic, managing director of DSCI.

The sixth cycle of OrbiMed’s Asia Partners fund included one with more than $1 billion earmarked for life science companies based on the Eastern continent.
OrbiMed has raised more $3 billion across two new private equity funds—including one specifically designed to support life science companies across Asia.
OrbiMed has also raised fresh funds for U.S. and European companies, for which the OrbiMed Private Investments X vehicle will have $1.9 billion in investment firepower, according to a press announcement on Thursday. Previous closes for this fund include a $1.86 billion raise in 2022 and $1.5 billion in 2021 .
Meanwhile, OrbiMed Asia Partners VI raised more than $1 billion to support companies across the Eastern continent. The vehicle adds to the $751 million raise for the fund’s fifth iteration in October 2023 and the $800 million sum from the fourth cycle in 2021.
OrbiMed managing partner Carl Gordon in Thursday’s statement pointed to the rise of China as one factor driving the innovation of new therapies. China-headquartered biotechs have accounted for 58% of all licensing deal value in 2026 so far, as compared to 26% for U.S.-based companies, according to a new report from Locust Walk. In 2023, the split was 14% for Chinese companies and 48% for U.S.

At the same time TCGX announced the new Asia-focused fund, the company revealed that it will open offices in Hong Kong and Shanghai “to take advantage of the explosive growth of early-stage drug discovery in China.”

After years of quiet maturation, new approach methodologies and emerging clinical success for cell therapies are fueling parallel momentum for induced pluripotent stem cells.
For more than a decade, induced pluripotent stem cells have generated significant interest thanks to their ability to give rise to any other cell type. Now, two trends are propelling this versatile tool toward transforming drug development.
Those trends are the rapid adoption of new approach methodologies (NAMs) and a growing body of clinical evidence in cell replacement therapeutics. These paths may seem independent, but they are in fact additive. Together, they are accelerating the maturation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) into scalable, clinically relevant platforms.
I have long appreciated the power of iPSCs, having participated in their development for decades—including in my current role working on iPSC manufacturing and clinical translation programs at FUJIFILM Cellular Dynamics. I now have the privilege of seeing iPSCs finally land in the spotlight.
Rising prominence
In 2012, iPSCs grabbed headlines as Shinya Yamanaka and John Gurdon were awarded the Nobel Prize for their work on reprogramming mature cells for pluripotency in the mid-aughts. Parallel work by James Thomson at the University of Wisconsin–Madison identified additional reprogramming factors and leveraged iPSCs to study rare diseases such as ALS and fragile X syndrome.
Initial broad success with iPSCs was found in toxicology screening, including iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes for a standard assay and for drug-drug interaction screening. iPSCs have now moved into batch release testing as well as contributing to drug discovery efforts. NAMs based on iPSCs are also used to develop mRNA/lipid nanoparticle combinations and viral vector–based therapies, to ensure they target the right tissues.
A breakthrough in the use of iPSCs in drug development came last year, when the FDA and the National Institutes of Health spearheaded a new push away from requiring animal testing in drug development, alongside similar European regulatory efforts. Animal models have always held only limited relevance for clinical success, and significant progress in iPSCs and other technologies has brought human-relevant modeling closer to reality. Engineering cells for automated compound screening on 384-well plates yields significantly higher throughput than breeding a mouse model.
FDA
FDA To Replace Some Animal Testing With AI, Human ‘Organoid’ Lab Models
Analysts at William Blair expect drug developers will continue to perform “at least some animal testing” on their investigational products. Though the process to phase out animal testing will begin “immediately,” no specific timetable was given.

·

·

The regulatory push away from animal models is speeding up adoption of a host of new technologies including 3D spheroids, organs-on-chips, microphysiological systems and other NAMs that rely on combinations of multiple iPSC-derived cell types. We at FUJIFILM Cellular Dynamics expect that demand in this area will continue to grow as NAM developers continue to phase in new models of disease, the blood-brain barrier, neuromuscular junctions and more. Customers have described numerous instances where iPSC-based NAMs laid bare issues based on human biology that were missed in animal models, saving significant time and resources in clinical development.
iPSCs hit the clinic
In parallel with the progress iPSC technology has made in the lab, advanced cell-based therapies have generated significant interest in their ability to treat and sometimes cure diseases that otherwise lack effective therapies. Initial cell therapies, especially patient-derived autologous approaches based on T cells and CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), reached the market quickly—if not entirely smoothly. To date, all have downsides when it comes to patient accessibility, with demand far outstripping manufacturing capabilities and affordability.
A recent announcement from Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare highlighted the progress of iPSC-derived therapeutics, granting the world’s first conditional approvals for two therapies based on the technology. Sumitomo Pharma’s Amchepry is a dopaminergic neuron replacement therapy for Parkinson’s disease, and Cuorips’ ReHeart uses cardiomyocytes to treat severe heart failure.
These won’t be the last. Multiple iPSC-based programs are progressing into or through late-stage clinical testing, including numerous other Parkinson’s treatments. BlueRock Therapeutics is currently conducting a pivotal Phase 3 trial of a human embryonic stem cell (hESC)-derived therapy for Parkinson’s disease, and is, in parallel, continuing to build out its next-generation iPSC platform. Aspen Neuroscience and Kenai Therapeutics are both preparing to enter Phase 3 for their respective iPSC-based Parkinson’s therapies. Other companies are targeting therapeutics for cardiac indications, retinal diseases and diabetes.
As with NAMs, therapeutic progress in this space over the past decade has largely flown under the radar. And as with NAMs, this progress has been enabled by success in manufacturing cells with consistent quality. Unlike commercial CAR T cell and HSC therapies, iPSC-based therapies can be derived from genetically stable iPS cell banks, in some cases based on the same refined protocols used to scale up dopaminergic neuron manufacturing for NAMs. They also differ from allogeneic therapies, which are still dependent on active and recurrent donors; iPSC therapies can be truly “off-the-shelf.” With a decade or more of safety data showing genetic stability of the parent cell lines, regulators are assured these products do not harbor genetic abnormalities that put patients at risk.
Lastly, with an established approach to commercial scalability, iPSC therapies have a path to patient accessibility that other cell therapies currently lack.
Similarly, developers avoid the patient-to-patient variability and difficulties in generating a sufficient therapeutic dose that can confound other cell therapy manufacturing efforts.
As with any new therapeutic modality, the field must still demonstrate long-term safety, particularly undergoing scrutiny of their in vivo genomic stability and any tumorigenicity, as well as immune tolerability. Regulatory pathways will need to evolve to keep pace with the unique characteristics of cell-based therapies. And manufacturing, while significantly advanced, must show it can scale efficiently.
With all of this said, the overall direction is clear. After years of hidden, incremental progress, iPSCs are entering a new phase defined by convergence across research, regulation and clinical development. Together, these advances may prove transformative for drug development.

Man Buys New Chevrolet Corvette Z06 Convertible for $170,460, Drives 843 Miles, Sells for $129,000
22 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
Even though I’ll be the first to tell you that the absolute sweet spot for a used C8 Z06, as far as the buyer is concerned, is that early six-figure mark... if you can get yours for around $105,000, it’s about as good as it gets. And yet, I absolutely love what I’m seeing here. It’s more or less my ideal Z06 spec, for what it’s worth.
Let’s focus on that word for a second. Worth . Because what I’ve done just now is I’ve gone on Chevrolet’s official configurator to build myself a brand-new 2027 Z06 Convertible with the exact same spec as this one, and guess what? You’d be spending roughly $180,000. So, I’m inclined to almost call this a steal.
The person who just landed this car at auction, did so for $129,000, plus a buyer’s fee – and this thing is basically still brand-new with just 843 miles on the clock. The original MSRP was $170,460. The seller took the hit, which was unavoidable.
Look, the economics of buying a used Z06 for over $130k+ are complex. That’s what this car cost when factoring in the buyer’s fee. But this also isn’t any regular Z06. It’s a 3LZ Convertible, with the Z07 performance suspension and carbon-ceramic Brembo brakes (courtesy of the Z06 Ultimate Performance package), but also the Visible Carbon Fiber Aero Package and the Carbon Fiber Interior Trim Level 2 Package.
Aside from the power-retractable hardtop, other exterior highlights include the several carbon fiber elements (splitter, rocker, high-wing spoiler, dive planes), as well as the black-finished 20” and 21” forged wheels with Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires. There’s also a front-axle lift system with memory settings, and you get Magnetic Selective Ride Control.
Meanwhile, inside is where you’ll find the heated and ventilated GT2 bucket seats in Jet Black leather and with Adrenaline Red stitching. Also the microsuede upper trim, a performance data and video recorder, carpeted floor mats, dual-zone automatic climate control, cruise control, a head-up display, a 14-speaker Bose sound system, plus several electronic driver aids such as rear cross-traffic alert, lane-keep assist, side blind-zone alert, and forward collision alert.
Photo: Bring a Trailer As for performance, we’re dealing with a mid-mounted 5.5-liter LT6 V8 , good for 670 horsepower and 460 lb-ft of torque. Everything gets sent to the rear wheels via an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission.
With the help of a 1-foot rollout, the Z06 can rocket to 60 mph (97 kph) in just 2.6 seconds. The top speed is 195 mph (314 kph), although the Z07 package can push that number down to 189 mph (304 kph).
Ultimately, I genuinely think this car was well-bought. Just a few weeks ago we saw this 2024 Z06 Convertible go for $122,000, and it had 13k miles on the clock – which is really far from delivery miles. But what do you guys think?

Ferrari, Lamborghini, Porsche: It's Time To Start Thinking About Rockets
41 photos
Photo: Tesla
Let's step back for a second and really look at what the all-new Tesla Roadster could bring to market once it enters production in about two years time. The fact that it can leap (instead of fly) like some early rendition of Superman, is nothing more than a distraction.
Try telling you wife enthusiastically how Tesla just unveiled a leaping, spinning car that people will be able to buy, and she’ll look at you as if you were a 14-year-old. Not that she doesn’t look at you like that already.
Sure, the fact that the Roadster can briefly take off and land is pretty wild. But it’s far from the bigger breakthrough here. For over a century, the car industry has struggled to generate as much grip as possible, using better tires, clever diffs, torque vectoring, just anything to improve acceleration. It’s usually the tires that limit performance. Just ask Mate Rimac or Christian von Koenigsegg.
What I see, when I look at the new Roadster , is possibility. Its cold-gas thrusters allow for a whole new way of applying force to a vehicle.
Rear-facing thrusters can generate forward momentum, but lateral thrusters could help a car change direction more efficiently. It’s properly fascinating. And I’d be way more impressed if the Tesla Roadster could achieve record levels of cornering speeds using controlled thrust, as opposed to performing wacky aerial stunts that benefit no one.
With that in mind, I think that this is the perfect time for the likes of Ferrari, Porsche, Lamborghini , and McLaren to develop their own thrust-assisted performance systems. Tesla doesn’t own that technology, because cold-gas thrusters aren’t anything new. Even a 12-year-old can understand the principle.
Gas is stored under high pressure and released through nozzles in whatever direction is deemed necessary. And because we’re talking about supercars and hypercars that already cost hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars, the additional expenses and complexity wouldn’t necessarily render such projects commercially impossible.
I’d like to see a thrust-assisted Porsche or Ferrari The first thing you need is the fan-based suction system. We know it works, because the Tesla Roadster isn’t the first automobile to use one. Any carmaker could implement such a technology, given enough resources.
Then come the lateral thrusters to generate sideways forces. This one is tricky, but possible – I mean, at this point, what is impossible?
Photo: Tesla Last but not least, the rear thrusters. Maybe you’ll use them as a sort of “push-to-pass”, or while having fun at the drag strip . I guess some forward-facing thrusters could help with braking, but now I’m just spitballing.
Like I said, in principle, any performance-oriented carmaker could copy and/or design variations of what Tesla just demonstrated. You can’t patent physics. Although, Tesla and SpaceX probably do have patents covering specific implementations, which is to be expected.
What I’d like to see from a breakthrough Porsche or Ferrari is something that uses small, precise thrust impulses to provide extra stability during extreme cornering, followed by an ultra-powerful burst of acceleration courtesy of the rear thrusters, coupled with the fan-based suction system.
Just put all that on the 2035 Porsche 911 GT3 RS and call it a day. Or in a new hypercar model. The latter is the more realistic scenario. I wonder if a thrust-assisted car would even qualify for all the currently viable production car lap records, or whether various motorsport entities would wake up feeling particularly litigious about it. That’s a conversation for another day.
Stop it, Sergiu, you’re losing it man! No. I. Am. Not. Is what I’d say using Ledger’s Joker voice. Here’s what you’re forgetting. BMW already demonstrated a fan suction system on the Vision Driving Experience prototype back in February of 2025. That thing had five electric impeller fans, generating roughly 1 ton of downforce even when the car was stationary. And then there’s the McMurtry Speirling, of course.
Photo: Tesla See, carmakers are already contemplating these things. They don’t need me to come up with any wild ideas – but they might need a kick in the rear from a rival brand, and that’s exactly what Tesla’s been known to do ever since they took the industry by storm with the original Model S.
What about the production Roadster? I don’t know. I won’t even speculate. I know some people think it won’t ever be allowed to leap in the air, and maybe it won’t. Or maybe you’ll only be able to do it under certain circumstances and in certain locations. I’m pretty sure you won’t be able to use it like a version of KITT’s turbo boost system , clearing traffic and other obstructions in the road.
Also, I’m not crazy about its styling. It’s a basic wedge-shaped, soulless sports car thingamajig, straight out of Cyberpunk or Blade Runner. I think we’ve had enough of these designs for a while.

China’s gold-backed exchange-traded funds held a record 304 tonnes at the end of September, even as bullion prices fell. ( Stock image by pla2na. )
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 16, 2026
China’s central bank bought more gold in September than in any month for almost three years, accelerating its bullion accumulation as the country’s jewellery market struggled.
The People’s Bank of China added 23 tonnes, taking third-quarter purchases to 63 tonnes, the strongest quarterly total since 2023, the London-based World Gold Council said in a report Thursday . Yet wholesale gold demand was 44% below its 10-year average during the quarter, weighed down by weak jewellery consumption.
“Persistently weak jewellery consumption was the main drag,” council researcher Ray Jia wrote. “The current macro conditions should remain supportive for bullion investment going forward.”
The divergence shows gold’s strength as a reserve and investment asset alongside weakness in consumer buying. Chinese gold-backed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) also accumulated bullion during the quarter, with holdings reaching a month-end record in September despite falling gold prices.
September marked the central bank’s 23rd consecutive month of reported purchases. Its official gold holdings reached 2,410 tonnes, accounting for 8.5% of total reserves, after additions of 103 tonnes since the start of the year.
Investment demand
Chinese gold ETFs added 11 tonnes in September, their third consecutive monthly increase, taking holdings to 304 tonnes. They accumulated 27 tonnes over the third quarter.
Weak domestic equities encouraged investors to diversify, while falling Chinese government bond yields reduced the income investors forgo by holding gold, the council said. Continued central-bank purchases also encouraged investment demand.
The buying forms part of a broader ETF investment surge that persisted through September’s bullion sell-off. The London gold benchmark fell 8.5% during the month, while the Shanghai benchmark declined 5.5% in yuan terms.
Chinese ETF inflows continued into early October as domestic stock-market weakness sustained demand for diversification, the council said.
Consumer squeeze
Banks, jewellers and other participants withdrew 234 tonnes from the Shanghai Gold Exchange during the third quarter, down 21% from a year earlier and well below the 10-year quarterly average of 418 tonnes.
The withdrawals serve as a gauge of wholesale demand rather than a direct measure of jewellery sales. The council identified persistently weak jewellery consumption as the main reason for the shortfall.
September brought a seasonal improvement as Chinese jewellers replenished inventories ahead of the National Day holiday in early October. Exchange withdrawals rose 48% from August to 92 tonnes, though they remained 22% below the year-earlier level.
Lower prices also encouraged purchases of bullion, the council said, citing anecdotal evidence of investors treating the retreat as an opportunity to buy.
Demand for jewellery, bars and coins improved during the late-September Mid-Autumn Festival and the subsequent National Day holiday. While the fourth quarter traditionally brings stronger jewellery sales, affordability and low consumer confidence could continue to constrain volumes, the council said.
